questions.prompt: An LRU cache is a map plus a doubly linked list behind one sync.Mutex. Profiling shows the lock is busy and a teammate proposes: "Get only reads, so take RLock in Get and Lock in Put." What is wrong with the proposal?
choices: Get moves the entry to the front of the list, so it writes shared state; concurrent RLock holders would corrupt the list
RWMutex cannot be used with generics
RLock is slower than Lock in every situation, so nothing improves
Nothing is wrong: the map reads are safe and the list move is atomic in Go
questions.explanation: In an LRU a hit reorders the recency list, which writes prev/next pointers; many RLock holders doing that concurrently is a data race that can corrupt the list. RWMutex works with generics. RLock is not slower in every case (it helps for read-only workloads), it is just invalid here. Pointer moves are not atomic in Go; only sync/atomic operations are. Real fixes: keep the plain mutex, shard, or batch recency updates as Caffeine/Ristretto do.

questions.prompt: You must make Get and Put O(1) for an LRU cache of 100k entries. Which structure choice achieves it?
choices: A hash map from key to a node of a doubly linked list ordered by recency
A slice of keys ordered by recency, moved to the end on every hit, plus a map for values
A binary search tree keyed by last-access timestamp
A min-heap keyed by last-access timestamp, with a map for values
questions.explanation: The map finds the node in O(1) and the linked list moves it to the front in O(1) because the node knows its neighbours. The slice version needs a linear scan to find the key's position (≈ 20 µs per op at 100k entries) and a memmove to shift. A BST and a heap are both O(log n) per recency update (and a heap cannot cheaply re-key an arbitrary entry without an index), so they are correct but not O(1).

questions.prompt: A full cache (capacity 1,000) holds 400 expired-but-unread entries and 600 live ones. A Put of a new key arrives. Which behaviour is best and what does it need?
choices: Evict the expired entry that expired first, found through a min-heap on expiry time
Evict the least recently used entry; expired entries will be dropped when someone reads them
Scan the whole list on every Put to look for an expired entry
Reject the Put with an error until a janitor goroutine has removed the expired entries
questions.explanation: Evicting a live LRU entry while dead data is retained wastes cache value and lowers the hit rate. A min-heap on expiresAt gives the earliest-expiring entry in O(1) (O(log n) to remove it). Plain LRU eviction keeps the garbage. A full scan per Put is O(n) on exactly the workload where the cache is full and busy. Rejecting writes turns a capacity decision into an availability problem and still depends on the janitor's timing.

questions.prompt: Select ALL statements that are true about calling an OnEvict callback from a cache's Put method.
choices: If the callback runs while Put holds the cache mutex and calls cache.Len(), the goroutine deadlocks
Collecting removals under the lock and invoking the callback after Unlock lets callbacks re-enter the cache safely
After this change, callbacks can run slightly after the removal and from several goroutines at once, and the contract should say so
Documenting 'the callback must not call the cache' is as safe as moving the call outside the lock, because the race detector will flag violations
questions.explanation: sync.Mutex is not re-entrant, so re-entering from the callback deadlocks. Deferring notification until after Unlock removes the problem structurally; the price is that notification is no longer atomic with the removal and may be concurrent, so it must be documented. A documented restriction is not enforced by the compiler, and the race detector does not detect lock-recursion deadlocks (those show up as hangs), so the last statement is false.

questions.prompt: You are testing TTL behaviour in an interview. Which approach gives deterministic tests of the exact expiry boundary (an entry with ttl 10s at t = 10s)?
choices: Inject a one-method Clock interface and advance a fake clock by exactly the TTL
time.Sleep for 10 seconds, then Get
Use a very small TTL such as 1ms and sleep 2ms
Call time.Now() inside the cache and assert with a generous tolerance
questions.explanation: A fake clock moves time by exact amounts, so boundaries (now == expiresAt) can be tested every run and the test takes microseconds. Sleeping for the real TTL is slow; tiny TTLs plus sleeps are flaky on loaded CI machines and cannot hit an exact boundary; a hard-wired time.Now() with a tolerance cannot test the boundary at all.

questions.prompt: The cache sits in front of a vendor call that takes 40 ms. A hit costs about 0.1 ms. At a 90% hit ratio, what is the average lookup latency in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: Expected latency = h × t_hit + (1 − h) × t_miss = 0.9 × 0.1 + 0.1 × 40 = 0.09 + 4.0 ≈ 4.09 ms. The miss term dominates: moving from 90% to 95% hits halves the average (≈ 2.1 ms), which is why eviction quality (not evicting live data for dead data) shows up in latency.

questions.prompt: Entitlement data is cached with a 5-minute TTL. A teammate refreshes expiresAt on every Get so that 'popular entries stay fresh'. Why is that a problem for this data?
choices: Hot entries never expire, so a revoked entitlement can be served indefinitely; TTL should bound staleness from the time of the write
It makes Get O(n) because the heap must be rebuilt
It breaks the LRU ordering
It is fine: the data is refreshed whenever it is used
questions.explanation: A sliding TTL measures time since last use, not time since the value was fetched, so an entry that is read at least every 5 minutes is never refreshed from the source of truth and can be stale for days (a security bug for entitlements). The change costs O(log n) per Get with a heap, not O(n), and does not alter LRU recency, which is separate from expiry. The last option confuses 'read recently' with 'verified recently'.

questions.prompt: A per-key token bucket stores `tokens float64` and does `tokens += elapsed.Seconds() * rate` on every call. At 10 requests/s with burst 1, a test probes every 10 ms for 100 simulated seconds and expects exactly 1000 admitted requests. It gets 999, and on production traffic the limiter is sometimes one permit short at the exact boundary. What is the sound fix?
choices: Switch to float32, whose coarser rounding lands exactly on 1.0 more often
Do the arithmetic in integers: count tokens in units of 1/Per tokens (nanoseconds times Events), so refill is elapsed*Events and every boundary is exact
Refill from a background goroutine with a time.Ticker once per interval, so the sum is never computed from small elapsed times
Compare with an epsilon (tokens >= 1 - 1e-9) so values like 0.9999999999999999 count as a full token
questions.explanation: Integer accounting makes the bucket's content exactly min(capacity, start + elapsed*Events) at any instant, no matter how the elapsed time is split into calls, and it lets RetryAfter be an exact ceiling. An epsilon hides this boundary but shifts it: the limiter now admits slightly early, and the error accumulates differently for other rates, so you are tuning noise instead of removing it. float32 is strictly worse: fewer mantissa bits means more rounding error, not less. A ticker goroutine replaces lazy refill with a leaked goroutine per limiter (or per key), drifts when the scheduler is late, and still adds floats; it also needs a Close that stage 1 does not have.

questions.prompt: A limiter refills lazily: `elapsed := now - b.last; b.last = now; tokens = min(cap, tokens + elapsed*rate)`. An NTP step moves the wall clock back one hour, and the limiter reads wall time. A minute later the clock is correct again. Which behaviour is right?
choices: Reset every bucket to full, because after a clock step nothing about the past can be trusted
Panic, because a clock that goes backwards is a bug in the host and should be loud
Time stands still at the high-water mark: the rewind adds no tokens, `last` never moves backwards, and the later catch-up adds none either
Treat the rewind as elapsed time and subtract tokens, so a key that misbehaved before the step stays punished
questions.explanation: Time as the limiter sees it must never go backwards: keep a high-water mark, treat a rewind as zero elapsed, and do not overwrite `last` with the smaller reading. The naive code does one of two things: it computes a negative elapsed and shrinks the bucket (denying legitimate callers), or it clamps elapsed to zero but still assigns `last = now`, so the later catch-up counts the same hour a second time and mints a full bucket for free. Resetting to full is the same free-burst bug, triggered by something an attacker may be able to cause. Subtracting tokens punishes callers for the host's clock and can deny traffic for up to an hour. Panicking turns a recoverable clock glitch into an outage for every tenant. In Go, time.Now() carries a monotonic reading and Sub uses it, so production code that keeps time.Time values (or an offset taken with Sub from an epoch) is mostly immune; the high-water guard is still needed for injected clocks and for readings taken before a lock is acquired.

questions.prompt: A public API limits per API key. Scanners send millions of one-off keys, and the limiter's key map grows until the pods are OOM-killed. You add key eviction. Select ALL statements that are true.
choices: Bounding memory requires a background janitor goroutine, because nothing else can notice that a key went idle
A fixed 60-second idle TTL on keys is safe for every limit configuration, because 60 s without a request is long enough for any bucket to refill
Dropping a key whose state equals a fresh one (the token bucket would be full by now, or the sliding window is empty) changes no future decision, so it is free
The cap on the number of keys protects you from key-flooding but is the wrong tool for ordinary housekeeping: idle reclamation should keep you far below it
Evicting the least recently used key when a hard key cap is hit fails open: a heavy user that was evicted gets a full allowance on its next request
questions.explanation: Idle reclamation is exact because the forgotten state is indistinguishable from a new key; a hard cap has to evict keys that are NOT idle, so it fails open (say so, count it, and flip it to fail-closed only where a vendor contract demands it). A fixed TTL is unsafe: a bucket with rate 1/hour and burst 5 needs five hours to recover, so a 60 s TTL hands its owner a full burst every minute, and the limit is effectively disabled; the safe TTL is at least the strategy's recovery time. A janitor goroutine is one option, but amortised sweeping when new keys arrive bounds memory with no goroutine, no Close and no timer, and an explicit Sweep covers quiet periods.

questions.prompt: An API returns `429` with `Retry-After: 1` to 5,000 clients denied in the same second. One second later the tenant's limiter admits 100 per second and 5,000 retries arrive within a few milliseconds of each other. 4,900 are denied again, with `Retry-After: 1`. What is the right response?
choices: Return a shorter Retry-After so clients come back sooner and the backlog drains faster
Raise the limit to 5,000 per second for this tenant, since the bucket is what rejected the retries

Spread the retries: jitter on the client back-off (and, where you control the server, randomise or stretch the advertised delay as the queue length grows), because an exact Retry-After is correct for one caller but synchronises many
Make Retry-After exact to the nanosecond, so each client comes back exactly when its own permit exists
questions.explanation: The advertised delay is exact for a single caller but identical for everyone denied at the same instant, so it turns a spike into a synchronised retry wave: an echo of the original spike each second until the backlog is gone. Jitter (or admission by queueing, as a server-side Wait would do) decorrelates the callers. A shorter Retry-After makes the echo more frequent. Raising the limit gives away the contract the limiter exists to enforce. Nanosecond precision is not what is missing: all 5,000 callers compute the same exact value, and only one permit exists at that instant.

questions.prompt: A limiter with one global mutex is the top entry in a mutex profile at 32 cores. You shard it: shard = hash(key) mod 32, each shard with its own mutex, key map and per-key state. A teammate worries that the limits are now only approximate. What is the accurate statement?
choices: Sharding is only safe if every key is hashed with the same shard count as the number of CPU cores, otherwise requests for one key can land on two shards

Per-key limits stay exact and atomic, because a key always lands on the same shard and is decided under that shard's lock; only cross-key aggregates (key count, a global cap, a stats snapshot) stop being atomic
Per-key limits stay exact only if each shard also takes a global read lock for the duration of every decision
Per-key limits become approximate, because two shards can each admit a request for the same key at the same moment
questions.explanation: A key maps to exactly one shard, so its check-and-take is still one critical section under one lock: sharding changes who contends, not what a key's decision means. What gets weaker is anything that spans keys: Len and Stats are read shard by shard, and a global cap is enforced per shard (cap/N each, rounded up). Two shards cannot both decide for one key by construction. A global read lock would put back the single point of contention that sharding removes. The shard count is arbitrary; the mapping only has to be deterministic for the lifetime of the limiter (and seeded randomly if clients choose the keys, so nobody can aim all their keys at one shard).

choices: The timer cannot be driven by a fake clock, so tests of Wait must sleep for real durations
Because select picks randomly when both cases are ready, the loop can spin without ever sleeping
A caller whose ctx is already cancelled can still take a permit, because ctx is only looked at after Check has run
Calling Check in a loop is unsafe, because a denied Check consumes permits and the bucket drains while waiting
When ctx is cancelled the timer from time.After keeps running until it fires, so a burst of cancelled waiters with long RetryAfter values pins that many timers (and their memory) on go 1.22
questions.explanation: Check ctx.Err() at the top of every iteration so a caller that has given up never takes a permit (select's random choice means a post-wake re-check is needed too), and use a timer you can Stop (injected, so tests can drive it) instead of time.After, whose timer lives until it fires on pre-1.23 semantics. The loop does not spin: after a random pick of the timer case it re-checks and, if denied, sleeps again for the new RetryAfter; the random pick only matters for correctness of the ctx check. A denied Check consumes nothing by contract, so repeated Checks do not drain the bucket.

questions.prompt: A vendor contract allows at most 600 calls in ANY 60-second period, and exceeding it is penalised. Your outbound limiter is a token bucket with rate 10 calls/s and burst 600 (it starts full). A traffic spike keeps the vendor client busy for the whole minute. What is the largest number of calls the limiter can admit inside one 60-second period? Answer in calls.
questions.explanation: A token bucket admits at most burst + rate x window in any window: 600 (the full bucket drained at once) + 10/s x 60 s (refill during the window) = 1200, twice the contract. To guarantee 600 per any 60 s with a token bucket you need burst + rate x 60 <= 600, for example rate 5/s with burst 300; or use a sliding-window log/counter, which counts the actual window (at the cost of O(limit) memory per key for the exact log). Average rate 10/s = 600 per minute is the number that makes the configuration look right.

questions.prompt: A 6-level garage admits at most ~1,800 cars an hour. The lot object keeps per-(level,size) free lists, a ticket map and a plate map, and each Park/Unpark takes about 1 microsecond of work. In review, a teammate proposes one mutex per level plus atomic counters for availability "for throughput". What is the soundest response?
choices: Accept per-level locks: any lock is faster when it is split, and atomic counters make Availability cheaper and still correct
Use sync.RWMutex for the whole lot, because Availability is called far more often than Park

Keep one lot-wide mutex: demand is about 1 operation per second against roughly 10^6 per second of capacity, and the invariants (plate uniqueness, ticket and free-list agreement, availability sums) span levels, so per-level locks would need a global lock for those anyway
Keep one mutex but only around the free lists, and let the plate map be a plain map that gates read without locking because plates never change
questions.explanation: The decision is driven by two numbers and by where the invariants live. Demand of about 1 op/s against about 10^6 op/s of single-lock capacity means contention is not a problem to solve, and the cross-structure invariants (a plate is parked once, a spot is free or held by exactly one ticket, Occupied + Free == Total) are cheapest to keep true when each mutation is one critical section. Per-level locks cannot protect the plate check, a cross-level strategy such as spread-across-levels, or a consistent Availability snapshot; separate atomic counters can show Occupied + Free != Total while a Park is half-applied. RWMutex does not help because Park and Unpark are writers, Availability is not the hot path here, and a read lock would not make the snapshot of several structures any more consistent than the plain mutex already does. Reading the plate map without the lock is a data race on a map that is written by every Park. Finer locking becomes the right answer only after a profile shows the lot lock hot, and even then the first move is one lot per garage.

questions.prompt: Park is written as: lock; if byPlate[plate] exists return ErrAlreadyParked; unlock; pick a spot and save the ticket to the database (about 5 ms); lock; insert the ticket into both maps; unlock. Two entry gates read the same plate within 5 ms of each other, for example a camera double-read. All single-threaded tests pass. What happens, and what is the fix?
choices: The second gate blocks on the lock until the first finishes, so it correctly returns ErrAlreadyParked; no change is needed

Both calls pass the duplicate check before either inserts, so the same car gets two tickets and two spots; the check, the spot choice and the insert must be one critical section (do slow I/O before or after it, not between)
The race detector reports the duplicate-plate bug, so running the tests with -race is sufficient to find it
Two tickets are issued but only one spot is consumed, so the only cost is a stray ticket; add a cleanup job
questions.explanation: The lock is released between the check and the insert, so both gates observe 'not parked' and both proceed: a check-then-act race across two critical sections. The fix is to make check, allocation and insert one critical section and to move slow work (the 5 ms write) out of it, for example by writing the record after the in-memory state is decided or by making the write idempotent on the ticket ID. Blocking on the lock does not help because the first gate has already released it. -race reports unsynchronised memory access; here every access is locked, so there is nothing for it to report, which is why this class needs a test that releases several gates at the same instant and counts successes. Each successful Park pops a spot, so two spots are consumed and the car occupies two spaces until someone notices.

questions.prompt: The owners want pluggable spot-allocation strategies (first fit, nearest to the entrance, spread across levels). Which Allocator contract keeps the lot's invariants safest and Park cheapest?
choices: The strategy receives the lot and returns the Spot it wants; the lot marks it occupied
The strategy receives a slice of every free spot that fits and returns one; the lot marks it occupied
The strategy receives the lot's mutex-protected internals so that it can lock exactly what it needs

The lot builds a short, ordered list of read-only pools (level, size, free count) that can take the vehicle, the strategy returns an index into it, the lot validates the index and pops the lowest free spot from that pool itself
questions.explanation: Choosing among candidates the lot built keeps the unforgiving part (is this spot free, does it fit, is it recorded in every index) inside the lot. A bad strategy can return a bad index, which Park rejects before changing anything, but it cannot hand out an occupied or non-fitting spot. The pool list has at most 3 x levels entries, so Park stays O(levels + log n). Returning a Spot the lot trusts turns one plug-in bug into a double allocation. Passing every free spot makes each Park O(n) work under the lock (about 50,000 items at an airport lot) and still lets the strategy return something stale or invented unless the lot re-validates. Handing the strategy the internals and its lock lets plug-in code deadlock the lot or break invariants, which is the opposite of a narrow consumer-side interface.

questions.prompt: Hourly pricing for a car: stays of at most 15 minutes are free (grace is a free pass, not a deduction); otherwise every started hour costs 300 cents; each started 24-hour block of the stay, counted from entry, costs at most 2,000 cents. What is the fee for a stay of exactly 50 hours? Answer in cents.
questions.explanation: 50 hours is not within the grace period, so pricing applies. It is two full 24-hour blocks plus a 2-hour remainder. Each full block costs the cap: 2 x 2,000 = 4,000. The remainder is 2 started hours = 600, below the cap, so the fee is 4,000 + 600 = 4,600 cents. Capping the whole stay once would give 2,000, which undercharges; ignoring the cap would give 50 x 300 = 15,000; treating the remainder's hours as a third capped block gives 6,000. Keep money in integer cents and do the ceiling division on nanoseconds, not on a float number of hours.

questions.prompt: Select ALL operations that should run OUTSIDE the lot's critical section in a well-structured Unpark/Park, because they are caller-supplied code whose speed or behaviour you do not control.
choices: Checking the plate map for a duplicate before assigning a spot
Calling Pricer.Price to compute the receipt's fee, after the spot has been freed
Popping the lowest free number from the chosen pool and recording the ticket in both maps
Reading Clock.Now
Invoking an OnPark/OnUnpark metrics callback supplied by the caller
questions.explanation: Pricing, the clock and caller callbacks are user code: a slow pricer under the lock stops every gate, and a callback that calls back into the lot deadlocks it (sync.Mutex is not re-entrant). They can run outside because their inputs are values (a copied ticket, an exit time) and the state change they follow is already complete. The duplicate check and the pop-and-record step are the lot's own invariant work and must stay in the same critical section; moving either out reintroduces the check-then-act race or a window where a spot is neither free nor held. (The Allocator is the documented exception that runs inside, because its choice must be applied atomically; that is why its contract says pure and fast.)

questions.prompt: Unpark is written as: lock; t, ok := byTicket[id]; unlock; if !ok return ErrUnknownTicket; fee = pricer.Price(t, now); lock; delete(byTicket, id); push t.Spot back on its pool's free list; unlock. A customer double-taps the exit button, so two exit gates redeem the same ticket at the same moment. What goes wrong?
choices: The second call returns ErrUnknownTicket, because the first call has already deleted the ticket
The second push panics because the spot is already in the free list, which surfaces the bug immediately
Both calls find the ticket before either deletes it, so the spot is pushed onto the free list twice; later, two different cars are given the same spot even though every single-threaded test passes
Only Occupied is wrong (it is decremented twice); the spots themselves are still handed out correctly
questions.explanation: The lookup and the delete are in two separate critical sections, so both goroutines can pass the lookup. Pushing a spot number onto a heap twice does not fail: the heap simply holds a duplicate, and two later Parks each pop it and get the same spot. A single-threaded test redeeming a ticket twice would pass, because the sequential second call really does find nothing. The fix is to look up, delete and free in one critical section, so only the first caller can find the ticket, and to test it by racing several redemptions and then filling the lot to prove every spot is handed out once. The claim that the second call simply returns ErrUnknownTicket holds only when calls do not overlap. A heap push does not panic on duplicates. And a duplicate free-list entry is exactly what corrupts spot assignment, so the claim that only the Occupied count is wrong is false.

questions.prompt: Stage 4: some Compact and Large spots now have EV chargers, and some cars need one. A car that does not need a charger should avoid EV spots when other spots are free, but may use them when nothing else is. In a design with Fits(kind, size), an Allocator over pools, and plain-data spots, which change is the best fit?
choices: Add an EV flag to spots and a needs-EV flag to vehicles; make the fit rule a predicate over both so a car that needs a charger only fits EV spots (a hard constraint); make pools (level, size, ev) and let the allocator express 'avoid EV spots when possible' as a soft preference
Create EVSpot and EVCar subclasses and override canFit in each, so the compiler enforces the rule
Make the avoidance rule part of the fit rule as well, so a car that does not need a charger never fits an EV spot
Introduce a Spot interface with a Charge() method and let every spot implementation decide who may park
questions.explanation: Hard constraints (a car that needs a charger must get one) belong in the fit rule; preferences (keep EV spots free for EV cars if possible) belong in the allocation strategy, because a preference must yield when nothing else is free and a constraint must not. Pools stay a small enumerable set, so Park stays cheap and the allocator still chooses among candidates the lot built. A subclass hierarchy adds types that carry one flag each, spreads the fit rule over several methods and makes combinations (EV truck, EV motorcycle) a class explosion. Putting the avoidance rule in Fits would make a non-EV car fail with ErrLotFull while EV spots sit empty, a user-visible bug caused by mixing policy into the constraint. A Spot interface with behaviour would be justified only if spots had behaviour that differs by implementation; here they differ by data.

questions.prompt: A key-value store keeps an undo log per transaction. Key "memo" does not exist. Inside a transaction a client runs Set("memo", "") and then Rollback(). What must Get("memo") return afterwards, and what does the undo record have to say for that to work?
choices: The empty string with found = true; restoring the previous value of an absent key means restoring a zero value
Absent, but only if the log stores the previous value as a pointer; a plain string cannot express absence, so Go stores cannot do this correctly
Absent (found = false); the undo record must say "the key did not exist", which is a different state from "the key held the empty string"
Either answer is acceptable as long as Len() agrees with Get()
questions.explanation: Rollback must return the store to exactly the state before the transaction, and absence is part of that state. The undo record therefore needs a presence flag (or a pointer/sentinel) next to the old value. Restoring "" turns a key that never existed into one that does exist, visible through Get, Len and Count(""). Go can express the flag perfectly well with a (value, existed) pair, so the third option is wrong, and the fourth is wrong because Get("memo") returning found = true is observably different from the state before the transaction.

questions.prompt: Key a is committed as "0". Level-1 transaction: Set(a, "1"). Nested level-2 transaction: Set(a, "2"), then level 2 commits (merging its undo log into level 1's). Finally level 1 rolls back. Level 1 already holds an undo record for a. Which merge rule gives the correct final value, and what is it?
choices: Overwrite the parent's record with the child's (latest wins); a ends as "1"
Keep the parent's existing record for a (first touch wins); a ends as "0"
Drop the child's log on commit because the parent already has the data; a ends as "2"
Append the child's record after the parent's and replay oldest-first; a ends as "1"
questions.explanation: The outer rollback must restore the state before level 1 first touched a, which is "0". The parent's record was taken then, so it is the older and correct one; the child's record ("1") is only the value at the child's own first touch. Letting the child overwrite the parent's record leaves a as "1", a value that was never committed. Dropping the child's log would be right only if rollback did not exist; the inner commit is provisional, so the outer rollback must still undo it, and "a ends as 2" ignores that. Replaying the parent's record and then the child's, oldest first, applies "0" and then "1" and also ends at "1"; with first-touch records there is exactly one record per key per frame, and the oldest one must be the one that survives.

questions.prompt: You maintain Count(value) incrementally, as a map from value to number of keys, while Set, Delete and Rollback change the data. Select ALL statements that are true for a correct implementation.
choices: Delete of a key that is absent in the current view must not change any count
Set of a key to the value it already holds must not increase that value's count
Rollback must apply the inverse count adjustments for every key it restores, using the same code path as a normal write
Count("") should include keys that are absent, because an absent key has no value and so equals the empty string
questions.explanation: Counts track keys, not operations: a delete of an absent key and an overwrite with the same value change no key's value, so an implementation that decrements or increments unconditionally drifts (a classic: Count goes negative after a rollback). Rollback restores old values, so it must adjust the counters exactly as a write would; routing both through one setter keeps them in step. The last statement is the absence-versus-empty-string trap again: absent keys are not counted by any value, including the empty string.

questions.prompt: Two sessions on a read-committed store with first-committer-wins on write-write conflicts, where the version of a key is recorded at the transaction's first WRITE to it. Session A starts a transaction and reads balance = 100. Session B sets balance = 150 and commits. Session A then computes 100 - 30 = 70, calls Set(balance, 70) and commits. What happens, and what is the fix?
choices: A's commit fails with a conflict, because B committed the same key while A's transaction was open
A's Set blocks until B commits, then proceeds with the fresh value 150, so the result is correct
A's commit succeeds and the result is 120, because the store replays the subtraction on top of the committed value
A's commit succeeds and B's deposit is lost; reading with a guard (GetForUpdate, or recording the version at read time) makes A's commit fail so it can retry
questions.explanation: A's first write of balance happened after B's commit, so the version A recorded already includes B's change and validation passes. A overwrites 150 with a value computed from a stale read: a lost update, which read committed permits. Recording a base version when the key is READ (an optimistic SELECT FOR UPDATE), or running the read-modify-write as a single atomic operation, closes it. A conflict error would require A to have touched the key before B committed. Nothing in this store blocks, and nothing replays arithmetic; the store only sees opaque values.

questions.prompt: To detect write-write conflicts at commit, a candidate stores, for each key a transaction writes, the VALUE the key had when the transaction first touched it, and compares it with the committed value at commit. Session A touches x (value "a") and plans to overwrite it. Meanwhile session B commits x = "b" and then, in a second commit, x = "a" again. What does the value-comparing design do, and what should be used instead?
choices: It reports a conflict, which is correct; values and versions detect exactly the same conflicts
It deadlocks, because both sessions hold the key; ordering the lock acquisition by key name fixes it
It sees "a" equals "a", reports no conflict and lets A commit over two intervening commits; per-key version numbers (a commit sequence stamped on each write) catch this
It reports no conflict, and that is correct, because the state A saw is the state it is committing against
questions.explanation: Equal values do not mean nothing happened. The ABA pattern (a, then b, then a again) hides two commits from a value comparison, and for the same reason it cannot tell a deleted-and-recreated key from an untouched one. A per-key version (or a global commit sequence stored per key, including for deleted keys) changes on every commit, so it flags the interleaving. Conflict detection here is optimistic and takes no locks, so there is nothing to deadlock. The last option confuses 'the value looks the same' with 'no one else wrote it': the interleaving the user cares about (first committer wins) was violated.

questions.prompt: A ledger transfer commits two keys at once: debit account a, credit account b, applied by the outermost commit under one critical section. An auditor goroutine runs v1, _ := s.Get("a"), then v2, _ := s.Get("b") and occasionally sees a total that is 10 too high. The commit code is correct. What is going on, and what is the right fix?
choices: The commit is not atomic after all; hold the store's write lock for every Get so reads cannot interleave with commits
The two Gets can straddle a commit: that is allowed under read committed. Read both keys in one call under one lock acquisition (an MGet) so the answer is one consistent state
The auditor needs GetForUpdate on both keys so that it blocks the transfer until it has finished reading
Nothing is wrong: totals only have to balance eventually, and the auditor should retry until two reads agree
questions.explanation: Atomic apply means no one observes half of a commit within ONE read; it does not make two separate reads see one instant. The auditor read a before the transfer and b after it, so it saw the old debit side and the new credit side, which is exactly a total that is too high. A multi-key read taken under a single lock acquisition fixes it (snapshot isolation would fix it for a whole transaction, at a higher cost). Taking the write lock for reads would serialise all readers for no gain over a shared read lock held across the one call. GetForUpdate in this design validates at commit and blocks nobody. 'Retry until they agree' is unsound: two reads can agree on a wrong total, and a bank cannot call money in flight a transient glitch.

questions.prompt: A store holds 200,000 keys. Each short transaction touches 3 distinct keys. Design A copies the whole map on Begin. Design B keeps a first-touch undo log. Roughly how many times more entry copies does design A perform than design B per transaction? Answer as a plain ratio.
questions.explanation: A copies all 200,000 entries per Begin; B records one undo record per distinct key touched, here 3. 200,000 / 3 ≈ 66,667. The ratio is not the point so much as the shape: A's cost per transaction grows with the store, B's grows with the transaction, which is why 20,000 Begin/Set/Rollback cycles on a 100,000-key store finish in milliseconds with an undo log and not at all with copies (2 billion entry copies).

questions.prompt: An in-process broker fans a ledger event out to four subscribers (statements, fraud, push, audit). Every Publish carries a 200 ms context and every subscriber uses policy Block with a 64-message queue. The audit consumer hangs. What should a sound broker do on the next Publish?
choices: Give the message to the three healthy subscribers immediately, wait for audit only until the 200 ms context ends, and return the context error
Wait for audit first, because delivery to subscribers must be all-or-nothing, and give the message to the others afterwards
Silently drop the message for audit, because a stuck consumer must never slow a publisher
Return success at once and let audit's queue grow without bound, so nobody ever waits
questions.explanation: Isolation means a stuck subscriber costs the others nothing: every subscriber that has room is served first (a non-blocking first pass), and only the Block subscribers that are full are waited for, with the publisher's context as the bound. All-or-nothing across subscribers would let one hung consumer stall the other three (and delivering to them afterwards still delays them by the whole wait). Dropping silently is policy DropNewest, which is only acceptable if the subscriber chose it and the drop is counted; under Block the contract is that data is not lost. An unbounded queue just moves the failure to an out-of-memory kill: at 600 messages/s a 64-message queue already fills in about 0.1 s.

questions.prompt: Publishers send on each subscriber's channel from many goroutines. Unsubscribe and Close must close that channel without ever panicking with "send on closed channel". Which design makes that impossible by construction?
choices: Exactly one goroutine per subscription sends on and closes the channel; publishers only append to a mutex-guarded queue and wake it
Publishers check a `closed` boolean immediately before every send, and Close sets it before closing the channel
Wrap every publisher send in a deferred recover() so that a panic from a closed channel is swallowed
Give each subscriber channel a very large buffer so that sends never block and so never race with Close
questions.explanation: Closing is safe only for the sender, and it is only safe if no other goroutine can still be sending. Making one goroutine the sole sender and the sole closer removes the question entirely; everyone else talks to a queue guarded by a mutex. Checking a boolean first is a time-of-check/time-of-use race: Close can run between the check and the send, which is the exact window that panics. recover() hides the crash but not the bug (the message is silently lost, and a data race is not made safe). A large buffer only makes the window rarer; a send on a closed channel panics whether or not it would have blocked.

questions.prompt: Ack timeout is 10 s. A consumer spends 8 s on message 1 while messages 2 to 5 wait in its queue. Which rule for starting each message's ack timer avoids spurious duplicates without lengthening the timeout?
choices: Start a message's timer when the consumer actually receives it, so queue time does not count against the consumer
Start the timer when the message is published, so the timeout measures end-to-end latency
Start the timer when the message is placed in the subscriber's queue, because that is when the broker handed it over
Start no timer until the previous message has been acked, so only one timer runs at a time
questions.explanation: The ack deadline is the consumer's processing budget, so it must start when the consumer has the message. If it starts at publish or at enqueue, messages 2 to 5 have already burned 8 of their 10 seconds before the consumer reads them and will be redelivered 2 s after it does, producing a duplicate for every message that waited. Starting the next timer only after the previous ack is the 'prefetch 1' discipline: it avoids the duplicate but serialises delivery and still needs a rule for when message 2's timer begins. A plain channel receive is invisible to the sender, which is why the reference puts a pump goroutine between the queue and an unbuffered channel: the moment its send completes is the moment of receipt.

questions.prompt: Select ALL statements that are true of an at-least-once broker with ack timeouts, redelivery and a dead-letter topic.
choices: A consumer can receive the same message ID more than once, so any side effect it triggers must be idempotent or guarded by a record of handled IDs
A consumer that keeps handled IDs in a process-local map is protected against duplicates after the process restarts
An Ack that arrives after the broker has already queued a redelivery should still settle the message and cancel the queued copy
Setting max attempts to unlimited guarantees that every poison message is eventually processed successfully
questions.explanation: Duplicates come from late acks, lost acks and crashes after processing, so consumers must tolerate them, and the late ack must count: the work was done, and rejecting the ack would just cause one more redelivery. A map in memory vanishes with the process, so after a restart the same webhook would be processed again; the record of handled IDs has to be durable and updated in the same transaction as the side effect (a unique constraint is the cheap version). Unlimited attempts do not make a poison message succeed; they make it loop forever and, with per-key ordering, block everything behind it. That is what the attempt cap and the dead-letter topic are for.

questions.prompt: A subscriber's ack timeout is set equal to its p99 handling time. The topic carries 600 messages/s and every message is handled correctly and acked, just sometimes slowly. Roughly how many spurious redeliveries (duplicates) per second does the broker generate?
questions.explanation: By definition 1% of messages take longer than the p99, and each of those outlives the timeout and is redelivered while the first attempt is still being processed: 600 x 0.01 = 6 duplicates per second. That is why the timeout is set well above the tail (a multiple of p99, ideally with the consumer extending leases for long jobs) and why consumers must be idempotent regardless: even a generous timeout only lowers the rate, never to zero.

questions.prompt: A ledger consumer must apply messages for the same account in order. Messages m1 (debit) and m2 (credit) share a key. m1's ack times out and is redelivered while m2 is already queued behind it. Which rule restores per-key order, and what does it cost?
choices: Allow only one in-flight message per key and hold later ones back until the earlier is acked or dead-lettered; a poison message then stalls its key and throughput per key is one message per handling time
Let the consumer sort incoming messages by publish sequence before applying them; this costs nothing because sorting is cheap
Disable redelivery for keyed messages; this keeps order and costs nothing because acks usually arrive in time
Spread each key's messages round robin across all members so no member sees two of them close together
questions.explanation: Redelivery re-sends m1 later than m2, so FIFO delivery alone cannot preserve order; the broker must not hand out m2 until m1 is settled. The price is head-of-line blocking per key: a handler that keeps failing holds up that account until the message is dead-lettered, and one key's throughput is bounded by its handling time. Sorting in the consumer needs unbounded buffering and can never know whether a missing sequence number is late or lost. Disabling redelivery gives up at-least-once: a crash then loses messages. Round robin across members does the opposite of what is needed: it makes concurrent processing of one account's messages likely.

questions.prompt: A broker keeps up to 20,000 messages in flight, each with its own ack deadline. Which scheduling design for redelivery is the better default?
choices: One timer armed for the earliest deadline, with the deadlines in a min-heap, re-armed whenever the earliest one changes
A time.AfterFunc per message, cancelled on ack
A goroutine per message that sleeps for the timeout and then checks whether it was acked
A loop that wakes every millisecond and scans all 20,000 pending messages for expired ones
questions.explanation: A heap gives O(log n) insert, cancel and 'what expires next', and needs a single runtime timer, so the cost does not grow with the number of in-flight messages and nothing is left running after an ack. A timer per message works but allocates and cancels 20,000 timers and needs a map to find them; a sleeping goroutine per message costs at least 2 KB of stack each (about 40 MB here), cannot be cancelled by an ack, and leaks until it wakes. A one-millisecond scan does 20 million checks per second to find, on most ticks, nothing; a coarser tick (for example 100 ms) is a legitimate simplification when redelivery precision does not matter, but it still costs O(n) per tick.

questions.prompt: A reminder service keeps about 500,000 delayed jobs pending (loan-payment reminders). The first version starts one goroutine per job: `go func() { time.Sleep(d); run() }()`. Which change fixes the most serious problem of this design?
choices: Keep the jobs in a min-heap keyed by run time, sleep one dispatcher on one timer for the earliest job, and hand due jobs to a fixed worker pool
Replace time.Sleep with time.After so that the goroutines are not blocked
Raise GOMAXPROCS so that the 500,000 sleeping goroutines can run in parallel
Replace the goroutines with a sync.Pool of reusable goroutines, one per job
questions.explanation: The design holds a parked goroutine (at least a couple of KB of stack, so on the order of a gigabyte here) for every pending job, has no way to cancel a sleeper except a flag it checks after waking, and when a million jobs share a minute boundary it starts a million concurrent runs with no bound and no ordering. A heap plus one timer keeps pending jobs as small structs, makes cancellation a heap removal, and the worker pool bounds concurrency. time.After does not change the number of waiting goroutines or the lack of a bound; it only changes how the wait is written. The sleeping goroutines are parked in the runtime and use no CPU, so GOMAXPROCS is irrelevant. sync.Pool caches objects for reuse and does not manage goroutines or bound concurrency; and one goroutine per job is the problem, not the fix.

questions.prompt: The dispatcher goroutine is asleep on a timer set for a job due in one hour. A caller now schedules a job due in 5 seconds. What must Schedule do for the 5-second job to run on time?
choices: Signal the dispatcher (through a channel with capacity 1) when the new job becomes the earliest one, so it re-evaluates and re-arms its timer
Nothing: when the hour-long timer fires, the dispatcher re-reads the heap and runs everything that is due
Start a new dispatcher goroutine for each job whose run time is earlier than the current head
Make the dispatcher wake every second and poll the heap, and have Schedule do nothing special
questions.explanation: The dispatcher computed its sleep from the heap head at the time it went to sleep. An insert that changes the head invalidates that computation, so the dispatcher has to be told. A capacity-1 channel with a non-blocking send also means that a signal sent while the dispatcher is busy is not lost. Doing nothing runs the 5-second job about an hour late, which is exactly the stale-timer bug. A dispatcher per job brings back unbounded goroutines and gives up the single ordering point (the tie-break by schedule order). Polling every second works but costs a wake-up per second forever and still adds up to a second of latency to every job; it trades correctness bugs for permanent overhead.

questions.prompt: A recurring job is scheduled FixedDelay with an interval of 10 s; its first run starts at t = 10 s. Every run takes 24 s. How many runs have started by t = 110 s (inclusive)?
questions.explanation: FixedDelay measures the interval from the END of the previous run. Run 1 starts at 10 s and ends at 34 s; run 2 starts at 44 s and ends at 68 s; run 3 starts at 78 s and ends at 102 s; run 4 would start at 112 s, after the cut-off. That is 3 runs. For contrast, FixedRate with SkipOverlap on the same job starts at 10, 40, 70 and 100 s (4 runs): the ticks at 20 and 30 s fall inside run 1 and are dropped, and the next kept tick is the first grid instant after the run ends. Counting 10, 20, ... 110 gives 11, which ignores that the job never overlaps itself; counting 4 uses the fixed-rate grid.

questions.prompt: A scheduler runs on a pool of 2 workers. Each job of type A schedules a follow-up job B and then blocks on a channel until B has finished. Two type-A jobs start at the same moment and both schedule their B. What happens?
choices: Both workers are blocked waiting for B jobs that can only run on a worker: the pool is starved and nothing makes progress, even though Schedule itself never blocked
Schedule deadlocks on the scheduler's mutex because it is called from inside a job
The Bs run on the dispatcher goroutine, so the jobs finish normally
The race detector aborts the program because a job calls back into the scheduler
questions.explanation: This is pool starvation: the dependency between A and B is a wait on a resource (a worker) that the waiters themselves hold. It needs no lock at all. Schedule only takes the mutex briefly to push onto the heap, so calling it from a job is safe (the lab tests this with Workers(1)); the deadlock comes from waiting inside the pool. The dispatcher never runs jobs, so option C is wrong by design (and running them there would let one slow job stop all timing). The race detector reports unsynchronized memory access, not re-entrant calls. The fix is not to wait inside a job: schedule the continuation from B (or B's completion callback), or use a separate pool for the dependent work.

questions.prompt: A timeout service schedules ≈ 20,000 timeouts per second, each due in 30 s, and ≈ 99% of them are cancelled within 50 ms because the operation finished. Cancel marks the entry as cancelled (a tombstone) and leaves it in the heap until it is popped at its run time. What is the steady-state problem, and what does the alternative cost?
choices: The heap holds about 600,000 mostly dead entries (20,000/s × 30 s), costing memory and log n depth; removing by stored heap index keeps only live entries and costs O(log n) per Cancel
Nothing: tombstones are O(1) and the heap size does not matter because only the head is ever read
The heap grows without bound because tombstones are never popped, so the process will eventually run out of memory
Tombstones break the (run time, sequence) ordering, so the live timeouts fire out of order
questions.explanation: A tombstone is popped when its run time arrives, so the heap contains everything scheduled in the last 30 s: ≈ 600,000 entries of which ≈ 6,000 are live. That is bounded, but it is 100x the live set in memory, makes every push and pop a couple of levels deeper, and keeps the closures and their captured data reachable for 30 s. Storing each entry's heap index and calling heap.Remove costs O(log n) per Cancel and keeps the heap at the live size. Lazy tombstones are a fine choice when cancels are rare or run times are near. Saying the heap size does not matter ignores memory and push cost. Tombstones are popped eventually, so the growth is bounded by the horizon, not unbounded. A tombstone does not change the order of the other entries.

questions.prompt: Your scheduler's Shutdown(ctx) is called during a deploy with a 30 s budget. Some jobs are running, some are due and queued for a worker, many are due tomorrow, and a vendor-sync job ignores its context and may run for minutes. Select ALL statements that a correct implementation satisfies.
choices: New Schedule calls fail with ErrClosed from the moment Shutdown starts, before the drain finishes
What happens to future-dated and recurring jobs is decided and documented (for example: dropped), instead of being left to whichever goroutine happens to exit first
When ctx expires, running jobs' contexts are cancelled and Shutdown returns ctx.Err() without waiting for jobs that ignore their context
OnError and other user callbacks are invoked while holding the scheduler's lock so that Stats stays consistent with what the callback sees
Shutdown waits for every job to return, however long that takes, so that no work is ever abandoned
questions.explanation: Refusing new work first is what makes the drain finite: otherwise producers can keep it from ever finishing. Future and recurring jobs need an explicit policy (drop, persist, or run early); with no policy the outcome depends on timing. On deadline the caller gets control back, and cancellation asks cooperative jobs to stop; the uncooperative one is abandoned and its goroutine exits whenever it returns. Callbacks under the lock are a bug: a hook that calls Schedule, Cancel or Stats (as a retry hook does) deadlocks, and a slow hook stalls every other operation. Waiting forever turns a stuck vendor call into a stuck deploy, which is the situation the deadline exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: The statement-generation job (fixed schedule: every month end at 00:00 credit-union local time) now runs in an in-process scheduler like yours, in 3 replicas behind a load balancer. At month end every replica fires the job and members receive three statements. What is the right fix?
choices: Make each run claim a lease or unique row keyed by (job, fire time, credit union) in the database so only one replica proceeds, and make the work itself idempotent per (member, period) in case the lease holder dies after partial work
Raise the worker count so that the three replicas finish the job faster than the duplicates can be sent
Switch the job from FixedRate to FixedDelay so the replicas drift apart in time
Run the scheduler in each replica but give each replica a different time zone
questions.explanation: An in-process scheduler has no knowledge of its peers, so every replica fires. The lease (or a unique constraint on the fire) elects one runner per fire; the idempotency key per (member, period) covers the case where the lease holder crashes mid-way and another replica takes over the same fire, because leases give at-most-one-holder at a time, not exactly-once work. More workers do nothing about duplicates. FixedDelay changes when runs start, not how many replicas start them, and it would also move the statement time away from midnight. Different time zones would generate statements at the wrong local midnight for the credit union, and still one per replica.

questions.prompt:
An expense-sharing service keeps balances as float64 dollars and rounds to two decimals only when it displays them. After a month, the 'settle up' screen shows one member owing $0.00 yet still lists a payment for them, and the sum of all displayed balances is one cent off zero.
What is the best diagnosis and fix?
choices: The error lives in the stored values: binary floats cannot represent most decimal cents, errors accumulate with every operation, and equality with zero stops being reliable. Store integer minor units (int64 cents) and convert only at the edges.
Display rounding is applied in the wrong place. Round to two decimals after every addition and the stored values will stay exact.
float64 has too little precision for this volume; switching to float32 with Kahan summation removes the drift.
The drift is harmless as long as the balances are compared with a tolerance such as 1e-9 instead of ==.
questions.explanation: Floats store the nearest binary fraction, so 0.10 is already slightly wrong when it is stored, and each addition rounds again; the error grows with the number of operations and depends on their order. Integer cents are exact, comparable and cheap, which also makes 'sum of balances == 0' a testable invariant. Rounding after every addition only moves where the error is hidden, and two different orders of the same expenses still round differently. float32 has even fewer bits, and compensated summation reduces but does not remove the error and still cannot represent 0.10. Comparing with a tolerance is how you stop noticing the bug: a cent is far larger than 1e-9, so a created cent would still be invisible to the check or would need a tolerance too large to prove anything.

questions.prompt:
Users a, b and c split a 100-cent dinner equally. a paid and is one of the three participants. The code computes share := amount / 3 in integer arithmetic and records that each participant owes share, and that the payer paid the full 100.
What is wrong with the resulting balances?
choices: They are +67, -33, -33: they sum to +1, so a cent was created from nothing and the zero-sum invariant is permanently broken.
They are +66, -33, -33: they sum to zero, so the only problem is that the payer is shown one cent less than they paid.
They are +67, -34, -33: they sum to zero, but the rounding favours the payer, which is acceptable.
Nothing is wrong: integer division always rounds toward the correct total, and the leftover cent is absorbed by the payer's balance.
questions.explanation: 100/3 = 33, so each of the three owes 33 (the payer's own 33 nets against what they paid): the payer is owed 100 - 33 = 67 while b and c owe 33 each. 67 - 33 - 33 = +1, so the ledger now contains a cent nobody paid, and every later operation adds exactly zero to the sum, so it never comes back. The second option has the wrong numbers (it would require the extra cent to be assigned to someone). The third has numbers that cannot arise from this arithmetic (nobody owes 34). The fourth is false: integer division truncates, and the remainder is exactly the cent that must be allocated explicitly (for example to the first amount%n participants in sorted-id order).

questions.prompt:
Four participants named a, b, c, d split a 10-cent expense equally. The ledger's rule is: sort participants by id, each owes amount/n rounded down, and the first amount%n participants in that order owe one extra cent.
How many cents does b owe?
questions.explanation: 10/4 rounds down to 2 cents each, and 10 % 4 = 2 cents are left over. The first two participants in sorted order (a and b) each owe one more cent, so a and b owe 3 and c and d owe 2: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10. The result does not depend on the order in which the caller listed the participants, which is the point of sorting before allocating.

questions.prompt:
A Simplify function takes net balances (positive: is owed, negative: owes; they sum to zero) and returns the transfers that settle everyone. It uses two max-heaps: repeatedly the largest debtor pays the largest creditor.
Select ALL statements that are true.
choices: For n non-zero balances it returns at most n-1 transfers, because every step fully settles at least one person.
It always returns the minimum possible number of transfers; that is why the heap choice is optimal.
Two runs on the same input return the same plan only if ties between equal amounts are broken by a total order such as user id, because Go randomises map iteration order.
After the plan is paid through Settle, the ledger's pairwise Debts() view is guaranteed to be empty.
questions.explanation: Each step moves min(creditor, debtor) so one of the two reaches zero and leaves the heaps; with n non-zero people the last step settles two at once, giving at most n-1 transfers. The determinism statement is right: building the heaps from a map visits entries in random order, so equal amounts must be ordered by something stable like the id, or the output (and any test of it) is flaky. The minimum is not guaranteed: finding it is equivalent to splitting people into the largest number of zero-sum groups, an NP-hard partition problem, and for balances +10, +9, -4, -6, -9 greedy uses 4 transfers where 3 suffice. Debts() records who transacted with whom, so paying a plan that has d pay a creates a new d-a entry while the old entries remain; balances are all zero but Debts() is not empty.

questions.prompt:
A shared ledger service passes every sequential test. In production, a monitoring job that calls Balances() every second occasionally reports that the balances sum to +40.00, and the next call reports 0 again. No data race is reported by the race detector, and the final balances are always correct.
What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
choices: A write is applied in more than one critical section (for example the payer is credited, the lock is released, then the debtors are debited), so a reader can see half an expense. Make validate-and-apply a single atomic step under one lock and have readers clone under the read lock.
Balances() returns a map, and Go maps are unordered, so the sum is computed over a different subset of users on each call. Sort the keys before summing.
The reader is missing a lock, which causes the sum to be read while a write is in progress. Adding RLock to Balances() alone is sufficient even if the writer still uses two critical sections.
Floating-point rounding in the sum; use math.Round on each balance before adding.
questions.explanation: A transient non-zero sum that heals itself, with correct final state and no race report, is the signature of a non-atomic multi-step update where every individual access is locked: each step is race-free, but the intermediate state is visible. The fix is to make the whole expense one critical section, so observers see the state before or after, never between. Map ordering does not change which users are summed; Balances() contains every user either way. A missing reader lock would produce a race report or a runtime crash on the map, not a clean +40.00, and adding RLock would not help while the writer still releases the lock halfway. The ledger uses integer cents, so floating-point rounding is not involved.

questions.prompt:
Another team writes a new 'split by income' strategy implementing the ledger's Splitter interface (Split(total) returns a share per user). The ledger will call it on every expense in a service where many requests run concurrently, and the strategy sometimes reads the current balances to decide.
Which design is right?
choices: Call Split before taking the ledger's lock, then under the lock validate everything the ledger depends on (users known, shares non-negative and unique, shares sum to the total) and apply. The ledger trusts nothing the strategy returns.
Call Split while holding the ledger's write lock so the balances it reads cannot change, and trust its result, since the interface documents that shares must sum to the total.
Call Split before the lock and trust its result; each strategy's own unit tests prove that its shares sum to the total.
Wrap Split in recover() so a panicking strategy cannot crash the service, and apply whatever it returns.
questions.explanation: User code must not run under your lock: a strategy that calls back into the ledger (here, to read balances) would deadlock on a non-reentrant mutex, and a slow strategy would stall every other caller. Split is a function of the total, so computing it first costs nothing. The invariant (sum of balances is zero) is the ledger's responsibility, so the ledger re-checks sums, signs, duplicates and users at the single commit point; a documented contract and the author's unit tests do not protect the books from the next buggy splitter. Calling Split under the lock risks the deadlock and the stall, and trusting its output leaves the invariant to whoever wrote the strategy; calling it outside the lock but still trusting the output keeps the invariant unprotected. Recovering from panics does nothing about wrong-but-valid-looking shares, which are the dangerous case.

questions.prompt:
A user deletes an expense that was added three weeks ago. Since then the group's membership changed and the team shipped a change to how percentage splits round. The ledger must remove the expense and keep every balance correct.
Which approach is correct?
choices: Store the exact shares that were booked when the expense was added, and reverse those (equivalently, append a compensating entry that references the original). Never recompute the split.
Re-run the split with the current rules and membership and subtract the result from the balances, so the reversal always uses the latest and most correct logic.
Delete the expense record, then re-run the split with the current rules for every remaining expense and rebuild all balances from scratch.
Refuse deletions after a week; only settlements can correct the books.
questions.explanation: A reversal must subtract exactly what was added. Storing the booked shares (or appending a reversing entry, as double-entry ledgers do) guarantees the books return to the precise prior state regardless of later changes to rules or membership. Recomputing with today's rules can produce different shares from the original, leaving residue cents or even touching users who were never charged. Re-splitting every remaining expense to rebuild the balances silently re-prices history whenever the rules changed since, and costs O(history) per deletion. Refusing deletions is a product decision rather than a correctness answer, and settlements would then be used to paper over a wrong expense, which corrupts the audit trail.

questions.prompt: An elevator car is at floor 3 heading up. Pending requests: a car call for floor 9 and a hall call at floor 6 with the DOWN button pressed. Nothing else is pending. Under the LOOK policy, what does the car do?
choices: Stops at 6 on the way up because it is closer than 9, then continues to 9
Passes 6, stops at 9 with the lantern pointing down, then returns and stops at 6
Stops at 6, reverses immediately to serve the down call, and serves 9 only after that
Passes 6 and 9 and travels to the top of the shaft before turning around
questions.explanation: LOOK keeps its direction while there is work ahead and stops only for car calls and for hall calls in its own direction. A down call at 6 is not on the way for a car going up to 9, so the car passes it, turns at 9 (the farthest request, with the lantern pointing down because work remains below) and serves 6 on the way back. Stopping at 6 on the way up is nearest-first reasoning: it opens the doors for someone who wants to go the other way and has no fairness bound. Reversing at 6 abandons the passenger already riding to 9 and would zig-zag under load. Going to the top of the shaft is SCAN, which wastes ticks travelling past the last request; LOOK turns at the farthest request.

questions.prompt: A first draft models the car as struct{floor int; dir Direction; moving bool; doorsOpen bool}. Which change most directly makes the state 'driving with the doors open' impossible to reach?
choices: Add a validate() method that panics when moving and doorsOpen are both true, and call it at the end of every public method
Guard every method that sets doorsOpen with a mutex so no goroutine can observe the combination
Replace the flags with one State enum (Idle, MovingUp, MovingDown, DoorsOpen) and assign it only through a function that checks a transition table
Keep the flags but write a unit test that steps a random workload and asserts the combination never occurs
questions.explanation: An enum whose values are the real situations removes the impossible combinations from the type, and the table makes every remaining change a checkable edge, so the property holds by construction. A validate() method detects the problem after the damage and depends on someone calling it. A mutex controls who sees the fields, not which combinations the code can produce: a single goroutine can set both flags. A random-workload test is valuable (the reference has one) but only samples behaviour; it cannot make the combination unrepresentable.

questions.prompt: A multi-car dispatcher re-evaluates every pending hall call on every tick and moves each to the car with the currently smallest ETA. In testing, passengers see a car start towards them and then another car appear instead, and some calls take longer than under the first-assignment design. What is the right fix?
choices: Re-evaluate only every tenth tick so that cars change their minds less often
Make the ETA estimate more accurate so the best car never changes
Let every car that is a candidate move towards the call and cancel the losers when one arrives
Assign each hall call once, when it first arrives, keep it with that car until it is served, and reassign only when the car becomes unable to serve it (out of service or halted)
questions.explanation: Stable ownership removes the flapping at its source: the dispatcher is consulted once per call, duplicates are coalesced before it, and the only reassignments are forced by a car leaving service. Re-evaluating every tenth tick only slows the flapping and adds a tunable parameter. A more accurate ETA cannot help because positions change every tick, so the argmin keeps moving even with a perfect estimator. Sending several cars towards one call wastes capacity and makes the other callers wait; it also needs a cancellation protocol. If you do want continuous re-allocation, it needs hysteresis (switch only if the new car is better by a margin), which is a different and measured design.

questions.prompt: An operator takes car 0, the only car in service, out of service for maintenance. The implementation removes car 0's hall calls and tries to dispatch each of them to another car; no other car is eligible, so the dispatcher returns 'none' and the code logs a warning and moves on. What is wrong, and what should it do?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because passengers will press the button again
The calls are lost; they should be queued with no owner and assigned, in arrival order, as soon as any car becomes eligible again
The calls should be kept on car 0 so they are served after maintenance ends, with the car still counted as in service
The operator's request should be rejected with an error whenever it would leave no car in service
questions.explanation: Removing a call from its owner and failing to place it again is the classic lost-request bug: the button lamp is lit and nobody is coming. Queuing it (owner unset, FIFO) keeps the invariant that every accepted call is either assigned or waiting. 'They will press again' turns a controller bug into passenger behaviour and breaks duplicate coalescing assumptions (the lamp is already on). Leaving the calls on a car that is draining or offline contradicts the point of taking it out of service and the car would refuse them anyway. Rejecting the operator's request is wrong in a real building: maintenance and safety take priority, and the controller must cope with having no cars rather than forbid it.

questions.prompt: Select ALL real problems with this run loop for an elevator controller: for { select { case <-ctx.Done(): return; default: c.Tick(); time.Sleep(time.Second) } }
choices: Cancellation is noticed only once per iteration, so shutdown can lag by up to a second
A test cannot control how many ticks happen, so it either waits for real seconds or races the loop
The period is one second plus the duration of Tick, and nothing decides what happens when a tick is slow
The loop pins one CPU core at 100% even though it sleeps
Calling Tick from the loop is a data race with ctx.Done()
questions.explanation: The loop checks the context only between sleeps, so cancellation is late; it owns the clock, so tests cannot inject ticks and must sleep; and its cadence drifts with Tick's own duration, with no explicit policy for slow ticks (a production ticker should drop ticks rather than queue them). The sleep prevents 100% CPU use (the version without a sleep would spin), so that choice is false. ctx.Done() returns a channel that is safe to read from any goroutine; there is no data race with Tick. The fix is to block on select { case <-ctx.Done(): ...; case <-ticks: c.Tick() } with the tick channel injected.

questions.prompt: The controller needs RequestHall to return the car it assigned. Select ALL statements that are true when comparing 'one mutex around the fleet' with 'one owner goroutine that receives requests on a channel'.
choices: With an owner goroutine, RequestHall needs a reply channel per request, so the caller blocks until the owner has been scheduled and has processed it
Both designs can make a tick atomic with respect to requests: a request is applied entirely before or entirely after a given tick
With an owner goroutine, a request sent after the controller has shut down can block forever unless the send also selects on a done channel or context
The mutex design cannot be tested deterministically, because tests would have to start a goroutine to drive ticks
The owner-goroutine design makes the race detector unnecessary, because no memory is shared
questions.explanation: An actor needs a way to hand the assigned car back (a reply channel) and pays a scheduling hop per request; it can still make ticks atomic because the owner handles one message at a time, as a mutex does; and its sends must handle shutdown or they leak blocked callers. The mutex design is deterministic to test: Tick() can be called directly by the test goroutine, no ticker goroutine needed. Even an owner goroutine shares memory (the reply values, the observer, anything closed over), so -race remains necessary; 'no shared memory' is a discipline, not something the language enforces.

questions.prompt: A car is at floor 3 moving up. Its farthest pending stop is floor 9. A new hall call arrives at floor 5 with the DOWN button pressed. Ignoring door time and intermediate stops, how many ticks (one floor per tick) until this car reaches floor 5 under LOOK?
questions.explanation: The car cannot stop at 5 on the way up for a down call, because work (floor 9) remains ahead. It rides 6 floors up to 9 and then 4 floors back down: 6 + 4 = 10 ticks. The plain distance of 2 floors (answer 2) ignores direction; 4 (the distance from 9 back to 5) forgets the trip up; 6 forgets the return. This is why a direction-aware ETA lets an idle car 4 floors away beat this one.

questions.prompt: A seat-hold service takes one mutex per requested seat, in the order the caller listed them, then checks and marks the seats. It passes every sequential test. During a sale, request R1 asks for [A1, A2] while R2 asks for [A2, A1], at the same moment, hundreds of times. What happens, and what is the smallest fix that keeps per-seat locks?
choices: Pairs of requests wait on each other forever (circular wait); sort the seat IDs and lock in ascending order
Both requests succeed and the seats are double-sold; wrap the status check in a second mutex
One request is slower, but no correctness problem exists; Go mutexes are fair so the waiting resolves itself
The race detector reports a data race; use atomic operations on the seat status instead of mutexes
questions.explanation: R1 holds A1 and waits for A2 while R2 holds A2 and waits for A1: a lock-order cycle, so neither ever proceeds. A total order on lock acquisition (sort, lock ascending) makes a cycle impossible. Double-selling is a different bug (check-then-act) and does not come from the locks being too strong. Mutex fairness only decides who goes first among waiters; it cannot break a cycle. There is no data race here, because every access is under a lock; the problem is the order, and atomics on status alone would not make a multi-seat hold all-or-nothing.

questions.prompt: A hold has ExpiresAt = T. The injected clock reads exactly T. A payment callback calls Confirm(hold) at the same moment a reaper goroutine calls Sweep. The spec says a hold is expired when now >= ExpiresAt. Which behaviour is correct for a well-designed inventory?
choices: Confirm always fails with an expiry error and the seats end up Available, whichever of the two runs first
Confirm succeeds if it gets the lock before Sweep and fails otherwise; either is acceptable because it is a race
Confirm succeeds, because the hold is still valid at the instant T and only becomes expired after T
Confirm fails with ErrUnknownHold if Sweep ran first, and with an expiry error otherwise
questions.explanation: With the clock frozen the verdict must be a function of the clock alone: expired is evaluated in one place against a 'now' read inside the critical section, so Sweep-first frees the seats (Confirm sees an expired hold) and Confirm-first reaps the hold itself before looking at it. Accepting either outcome makes behaviour depend on scheduling and cannot be tested. Treating T as still valid contradicts the stated rule now >= ExpiresAt. Reporting ErrUnknownHold after a sweep makes the error depend on whether a background job ran, so a late payment callback could not tell 'expired, refund' from 'never existed'.

questions.prompt: Select ALL designs for a multi-seat Hold that are all-or-nothing and cannot deadlock (ignore performance).
choices: One mutex per event; under it, validate every requested seat and only then mark them
Per-seat mutexes acquired in ascending seat-ID order and held across validation and marking
Per-seat mutexes acquired in the order the caller listed the seats
Check that all seats are available under the event lock, release it, then lock each seat to mark it held
questions.explanation: A single event lock has no second lock to wait for, and validating before mutating needs no rollback. Sorted per-seat locking imposes a global order, so no cycle can form, and holding them across validate-and-mark keeps the operation atomic. Request-order locking has the circular-wait problem for requests such as [A1, A2] and [A2, A1]. Checking, unlocking and then marking is check-then-act: another request can take a seat in the gap, so the hold is neither all-or-nothing nor exclusive.

questions.prompt: ConfirmWithKey(hold H, key K) succeeded and the customer was charged. The payment provider retries the same callback 20 minutes later; H's TTL was 10 minutes. What should the inventory return?
choices: The original booking, unchanged, with no second charge
ErrHoldExpired, since the hold's TTL has passed
A new booking for the same seats if they are still free
ErrAlreadyConfirmed, because the hold was already used
questions.explanation: Idempotency means the same request gets the same answer. Once confirmed, the hold is a booking, and bookings do not expire; the retry must return the original booking without a second effect. ErrHoldExpired would turn a success into an apparent failure and could trigger a refund of a valid order. Creating a new booking is a double charge. ErrAlreadyConfirmed is correct for a different key or a keyless Confirm on a confirmed hold, but with the same key it is exactly the case idempotency exists to answer with the stored result.

questions.prompt: A candidate records the idempotency key only AFTER a successful confirm, using a check like 'if key seen: return stored; else confirm and store'. Two callbacks arrive concurrently carrying the same key but naming different holds H1 and H2. What can go wrong?
choices: Both pass the 'not seen' check, both confirm, and one key yields two bookings and two charges
Neither confirms, because each waits for the other to store the key
