H2's callback always wins, because later arrivals overwrite the stored key
Nothing; the second confirm fails because the seats of H2 are already booked
questions.explanation: Check and store are separate steps, so both goroutines can observe 'not seen' before either stores: a check-then-act race on the key registry itself. The fix is to bind the key to its hold before examining the hold, under the same lock that serialises the operation, so the loser gets a key-reuse error. There is no mutual waiting involved, so there is no deadlock. Overwriting is not what happens; both succeed. H1 and H2 hold different seats, so booking one does not stop the other.

questions.prompt: Release(holdA) deletes the hold from the lookup map but leaves its entry in the expiry queue. Bob then holds the same seat. When holdA's original deadline passes, the reaper pops the stale entry. Which outcome follows, and which two safeguards prevent it?
choices: Bob's seat is freed and can be sold again; remove the hold from the expiry index on every exit path and free a seat only if the hold still owns it
Nothing happens, because the reaper skips holds that are missing from the lookup map by construction
The reaper panics on the missing map entry; recover from it in the reaper loop
Alice is refunded twice; add an idempotency key to Release
questions.explanation: The stale entry still names the seat, so the reaper marks it Available while Bob's live hold believes it owns it: an oversell waiting to happen. Two safeguards remove the class of bug: take the hold out of every index when it leaves the active set, and make freeing owner-checked (seat.holder == hold). The reaper is not protected by the map lookup unless the code is written that way; assuming it is exactly how the bug ships. Recovering from a panic is not the failure mode here. Release moves no money, so idempotency keys do not apply to it.

questions.prompt: A Hold holds one event's mutex for about 2 microseconds (a few map lookups and a heap push). Ignoring everything else, roughly how many Hold calls per second can ONE event sustain on one core? Answer in holds/s.
questions.explanation: One second contains 1,000,000 microseconds; at 2 microseconds per serialised critical section that is about 500,000 operations per second. Real systems sit well below that, because the network hop in front (about 100 microseconds) and the payment path dominate, which is why a hot sale needs admission control rather than a fancier lock.

questions.prompt: An in-memory file system stores files in a map[string][]byte keyed by full path. Its RemoveAll(dir) deletes every key with strings.HasPrefix(key, dir). Tests pass when run one at a time, but when ten tenants' tests run in parallel, one in nine fail with 'file not found'. Which is the root cause?
choices: A string prefix is not a path prefix: RemoveAll("/exports/cu-1") also deletes /exports/cu-10 through cu-19
The map needs a sync.RWMutex; the failures are data races on the map
Keys must be lower-cased, because different tenants' paths differ only in case
RemoveAll must run in a separate goroutine so that deletion does not block readers
questions.explanation: The failures are sibling deletions: '/exports/cu-1' is a string prefix of '/exports/cu-10', so one test cleans up another tenant's files. The fix is to compare path components (or model the hierarchy as a tree so a sibling can never be confused with a descendant). Missing locks would crash with 'concurrent map writes' or be flagged by -race rather than produce 'not found' for specific siblings. Case has nothing to do with it, and running deletion in a goroutine makes the sibling-deletion bug harder to see, not fixed.

questions.prompt: Your file system's Walk(root, fn) takes mu.RLock(), traverses, and calls fn for each node before returning. A caller's fn calls fs.WriteFile(p+".bak", data). What happens?
choices: WriteFile waits for the write lock while its own goroutine still holds the read lock: it deadlocks
It works: a goroutine that holds RLock may upgrade to Lock
WriteFile panics with 'sync: Lock called while RLock held'
It works but fn sees the old tree, because the write is queued until Walk returns
questions.explanation: sync.RWMutex has no upgrade and is not re-entrant: Lock waits for every reader to release, including the goroutine that is waiting. The result is a self-deadlock (a hang in a server; 'all goroutines are asleep' in a test). There is no panic for this case, and the write cannot be 'queued' because the caller blocks inside the same call chain. The fix is to snapshot under the lock and call fn after releasing it.

questions.prompt: A file system enforces a total byte quota. Writers call WriteFile concurrently. Select ALL that must happen inside one critical section for the quota to hold.
choices: Computing the size delta from the existing file's length
Comparing used+delta against the quota
Updating the file's data and the used counter
Parsing and cleaning the path string
questions.explanation: The delta depends on the current file size, which other writers change, so reading it, comparing against the quota and applying the effect must be one atomic step; otherwise several writers all pass the check on the same free space and the quota is exceeded. Path parsing touches only the caller's own string, so it should happen before taking the lock to keep the critical section short.

questions.prompt: To let unrelated renames run in parallel you give every directory node its own mutex. Two goroutines run Rename("/p", "/q/p") and Rename("/q", "/p/q") at the same moment. Which pair of failures can occur?
choices: Deadlock from opposite lock ordering, or both succeeding and leaving /p and /q as unreachable children of each other
Only a data race on node names, which -race would report; the tree itself stays valid
Only a lost update on the used-bytes counter
Nothing: each rename locks its own source, so they cannot interfere
questions.explanation: Each rename needs to lock both a source parent and a destination parent; taking them in opposite orders deadlocks. If instead each rename does its 'is the destination inside the source?' check before the other has finished, both checks pass and both succeed, leaving a cycle detached from the root. A single tree-wide lock (or a global rename lock plus ordered per-node locks) prevents both. The other options understate the problem: this is a logical race, not just a data race, and it concerns tree shape rather than only counters.

questions.prompt: In this file system, Rename("/a", "/b") is called where /a is a file and /b is an existing non-empty directory, following POSIX rename semantics. What is the result?
choices: An error (EISDIR-style): a file cannot replace a directory
Success: /b is replaced by the file and its contents are deleted
Success: /a is moved inside /b as /b/a
An error only because /b is non-empty; an empty directory would be replaced
questions.explanation: POSIX rename never replaces a directory with a non-directory (EISDIR) and never replaces a non-directory with a directory (ENOTDIR). A directory may replace only an EMPTY directory (ENOTEMPTY otherwise). Moving a source into the destination directory is what the mv command does, not what rename(2) does. Non-emptiness is irrelevant to the file-onto-directory case, which fails either way.

questions.prompt: Which statement about resolving ".." in paths like "/a/b/../c" by calling path.Clean before any lookup is correct?
choices: It is correct only because there are no symbolic links; with a link, '..' must be applied to the resolved directory during the walk
It is always correct, because '..' is purely syntactic
It is never correct; every '..' must be resolved by looking up the parent node
It is correct only if the path is relative
questions.explanation: With symlinks, /a/b/.. depends on where b points: the kernel resolves b first and then goes to the parent of its target. Without links, the parent of /a/b is always /a, so textual cleaning is exact. Relative paths are not valid input here, and a tree without links does not need parent pointers for '..'.

questions.prompt: A flat-map file system lists a directory by scanning all keys and checking each for the right parent. The map has 200,000 keys and a prefix/parent check costs about 15 ns per key. How long does one listing take? Answer in milliseconds.
questions.explanation: 200,000 keys x 15 ns = 3,000,000 ns = 3 ms, held under the lock, per listing. At 300 listings per second that is about 0.9 of a core spent on scans. A tree makes the same listing cost O(children), around a microsecond for a handful of entries.

questions.prompt: A test runs 4 goroutines that each call Walk("/") in a loop, counting files, while another goroutine renames /a/f to /b/f and back 2,000 times. The test requires every Walk to count exactly 1 file. Which Walk implementation passes?
choices: Copy the whole subtree's entries under one RLock, release it, then call the callback
RLock each directory in turn, copy its children, unlock, and recurse
No lock in Walk, because renames only move a pointer
RLock only the root while traversing the children
questions.explanation: Only a snapshot taken at one instant guarantees the file is seen once: a concurrent rename cannot appear half done. With per-directory locking, Walk can read /a before the file leaves it and /b after it arrives, counting it twice, or the reverse, counting it zero times. No lock at all is a data race on the child maps, and locking just the root does not protect the child directories' maps.

questions.prompt: A service logs ~12 lines per request at 2,000 req/s and ships each line synchronously to a log aggregator. The aggregator slows from 5 ms to 800 ms per call and the service falls over. Which redesign addresses the cause without creating a new failure?
choices: A bounded queue with batching, a drop policy that counts what it sheds, and a background worker that talks to the aggregator
Start a goroutine per log line so callers never wait
Replace the sink with an unbounded in-memory slice and drain it when the aggregator recovers
Keep it synchronous but add a 10-second client timeout to every call
questions.explanation: The outage is caused by coupling the request path to the log destination. A bounded queue decouples them, batching cuts calls from ~24,000/s to tens per second, and an explicit drop policy bounds memory. A goroutine per line just moves the pile-up into ~19,000+ live goroutines (and OOM when calls hang until the timeout). An unbounded slice grows ~7 MB/s and OOMs in minutes. A longer timeout keeps every request thread parked for up to 10 s per line, which is worse.

questions.prompt:
A logger's With is: child := *l; child.fields = append(l.fields, fields...); return &child.

base := root.With(f1).With(f2).With(f3)
s1 := base.With(f4)
s2 := base.With(f5)

What fields does an entry logged through s1 carry?
choices: f1, f2, f3, f5: s2's With overwrote the spare slot s1 used, because they share one backing array
f1, f2, f3, f4, as intended
It is a data race that -race will always report
questions.explanation: append grows capacity 1, 2, 4, so base has length 3 and capacity 4. Both children append into the same spare slot and end up viewing the same array; the later write wins. With one child per parent the bug is invisible. -race does not report it when the two With calls happen sequentially: it is an aliasing bug, not a data race. The intended result needs a fresh allocation and copy in With.

questions.prompt: A service produces 24,000 log lines per second. The shipper accepts batches of 500 lines. How many shipper calls per second does batching need? Answer in calls per second.
questions.explanation: 24,000 lines/s divided by 500 lines per batch = 48 calls/s, versus 24,000 calls/s unbatched. Linger bounds the delay for a partial batch at low traffic, so the real number is slightly higher at off-peak.

questions.prompt: AsyncSink.Close(ctx) is called with a 2 s deadline while the destination's WriteBatch has been blocked for a minute, with 40 entries queued behind the in-flight batch of 3. Which behaviour is best?
choices: Stop waiting at the deadline, tell the worker to abandon the queue (counted as dropped), cancel retry sleeps, and return an error that wraps ctx.Err() and reports the 43 undelivered entries
Keep waiting until WriteBatch returns, so that no entry is ever lost
Return nil at the deadline and leave the worker running in the background
Panic, so that the supervisor restarts the process and the problem is visible
questions.explanation: Close cannot interrupt foreign code, so it must bound its own wait and make the loss explicit: abandon, cancel the sleeps the worker owns, and report a count. Waiting forever is the hang the deadline exists to prevent. Returning nil is a lie, and the worker would keep draining to a dead destination after the caller believes the sink is closed. Panicking in a shutdown path turns a degraded dependency into a crash.

questions.prompt: A batching worker starts a linger timer when the first entry of a batch arrives. The batch fills and is flushed by size, but the code neither stops that timer nor forgets its channel. What is the practical effect on the next batch?
choices: The old timer fires early relative to the new batch, producing cut-short batches and more destination calls, with no entry lost
Entries are lost, because the timer flushes an empty batch
The program deadlocks, because the timer channel has no reader
Nothing: timers are garbage-collected as soon as the batch is flushed
questions.explanation: A stale timer measures the wrong batch's age, so the next batch is flushed early. Delivery stays correct, so correctness tests pass, but the batching benefit erodes and the destination sees more calls. The fix is one timer per batch, stopped and its channel dropped when the batch leaves; a test that fires the stale timer on purpose catches it. Nothing is lost or deadlocked, and an unstopped timer is not collected before it fires.

questions.prompt: A login endpoint logs the submitted username verbatim in a line-oriented text log. An attacker submits "bob\n2026-03-04T05:06:07Z ERROR admin password reset". What is the problem, and what is the standard defence in the log formatter?
choices: The newline forges a second, authentic-looking line (log injection); quote or escape control characters so one entry is always one line
The line becomes too long; truncate messages at 256 bytes
The timestamp is duplicated; deduplicate entries by timestamp
Nothing is wrong, because the logger holds a mutex while writing
questions.explanation: Line-oriented logs are parsed by humans and tools line by line, so an embedded newline lets user input fabricate entries (CWE-117). The mutex only prevents interleaving between entries; it does nothing about a single entry containing a newline. Truncation and deduplication do not stop forged lines.

questions.prompt: A team must record every funds-transfer audit event for a regulator. Someone proposes using the async logging pipeline with a DropOldest queue and retries, because 'it is already there'. What is the right response?
choices: Reject it: audit events must be written in the same database transaction as the transfer (outbox) and shipped at-least-once; keep the lossy logger for diagnostics only
Accept it, but raise the queue size to 1 million entries
Accept it, and switch the policy to Block so nothing is dropped
Accept it, but call Flush after every entry
questions.explanation: An in-memory queue is lost on a crash or a restart no matter how big it is or which policy it uses; Block only moves the failure into the request path, and Flush after every entry makes it synchronous without making it durable. A transactional outbox makes the audit record exactly as durable as the business change. The debug log can still exist beside it as a convenience.

questions.prompt: After closing an async sink, Stats reports Received = 1000, Written = 950, Dropped = 40, Failed = 0. What does this tell you?
choices: Ten accepted entries are unaccounted for: some path discards entries without counting them
Everything is fine: 950 + 40 is close enough to 1000
Ten entries are still in the queue, which Close leaves behind by design
The Received counter is over-counting by ten, which is harmless
questions.explanation: Once the sink is quiescent every accepted entry must end in exactly one of Written, Dropped or Failed. A gap means entries vanished silently (for example a recovered panic or an abandoned batch that was never counted). Close drains the queue, so leftovers would be a bug too. Counters that do not add up make drops unmeasurable, which is the one thing a lossy pipeline must not be.

questions.prompt: Select ALL statements that are true for a bounded async queue whose destination is stuck and whose queue is full.
choices: With DropNewest the caller's Write returns immediately and the entries that survive are the oldest ones
With DropOldest the caller's Write returns immediately and the entries that survive are the newest ones
With Block the caller's latency becomes the destination's latency
With Block, a Close call can release the blocked callers, which then receive an error
questions.explanation: DropNewest sheds the incoming entry and keeps what is queued; DropOldest evicts the head and keeps the freshest; both return at once. Block parks the caller until there is room, so the caller inherits the destination's latency. A correct Close must wake those parked callers with an error (ErrClosed), otherwise shutdown leaves goroutines stuck forever.

questions.prompt: Why does the async sink use exactly one background goroutine to call the destination, rather than a pool?
choices: It keeps batches in queue order and gives retries, the timer and batch ownership a single owner, at the cost of destination parallelism
Go forbids calling an interface method from more than one goroutine
A pool would make the queue lock unnecessary
A single goroutine is always faster than several
questions.explanation: A single worker serialises destination calls, so ordering, retry state and the linger timer have one owner and there are no concurrent WriteBatch calls to reason about. The cost is that throughput is bounded by one destination call at a time; if that becomes the bottleneck you add a pool deliberately, accepting weaker ordering. Go has no such restriction, a pool still needs the queue lock, and one goroutine is not always faster.

questions.prompt: A vending machine's Select holds its mutex while the motor runs (about 2 s). To stop blocking other callers, a developer releases the mutex around the motor call but adds no new state, so the machine still reports HasMoney meanwhile. What can go wrong?
choices: Cancel can succeed while the item is dropping, so the customer gets both the item and a refund
The motor call now runs twice
The mutex becomes re-entrant and callers deadlock
Go's race detector reports a data race on the slot map even though every access takes the lock
questions.explanation: With no state marking the gap, Cancel (or a second Select) is still legal while the item drops, so the customer can receive the item and a refund, which is check-then-act across an unlocked gap. The fix is a Dispensing state: phase 1 under the lock reserves stock and enters Dispensing, the motor runs unlocked, phase 3 commits or rolls back; other events get ErrInvalidState immediately. The other options are not consequences: releasing the lock does not make the motor call slower or the mutex re-entrant, and it does not by itself create a data race on the maps as long as every access still takes the lock.

questions.prompt: The change box has one quarter and three dimes. A customer paid 100 cents for a 70-cent item, so 30 cents of change is owed. A greedy 'largest coin first' routine reports it cannot make change. Which statement is correct?
choices: The machine should dispense the item and give 25 cents, keeping the 5-cent difference
The sale is wrongly refused: three dimes make exactly 30 cents, so the algorithm must search combinations within the available stock
The machine must be restocked with a nickel before this sale can ever be served
The refusal is correct: change must start with the largest coin available
questions.explanation: Three dimes make exactly 30 cents, so a sale that should succeed is refused. Greedy is only safe for canonical coin systems with unlimited supply; with finite stock it can take the quarter and then be stuck needing a nickel. A bounded coin-change DP (or memoised backtracking) finds the dime combination. 'Correctly refused' is wrong because an exact combination exists; adding more quarters is not required; and rounding change to the nearest 5 cents changes the product rules without asking.

questions.prompt: A vending machine protects its state with one mutex and uses a Dispenser (motor), a card Gateway and notification listeners. Select ALL calls that should be made while the mutex is NOT held.
choices: Calling Dispenser.Dispense
Reserving stock (quantity minus one) for the sale
Calling Gateway.Capture
Running notification listeners
questions.explanation: Anything slow or user-supplied must run outside the lock: the motor call (seconds), the gateway's Capture/Void (network), and listeners (arbitrary code that may re-enter the machine or block). Reserving stock is the opposite: it is a quick state change that must be atomic with the validation and the move to Dispensing, so it happens under the lock.

questions.prompt: A machine is built from state types that each embed a baseState which returns ErrInvalidState for every event. The interviewer adds a new event, PayByCard, that only Idle accepts. What is the minimal change?
choices: Add a case for PayByCard to every state type's methods
Add the method to the interface and baseState (reject), and override it in Idle only
Add a boolean 'cardMode' to the machine and check it in every method
Add a package-level switch on the state value that handles PayByCard
questions.explanation: Add PayByCard to the state interface and a rejecting default to baseState, then override it in the Idle state only. Every other state inherits the rejection, so no existing state is edited and the new event is safe by default in states you forgot. Editing all states duplicates the default and invites omissions; a boolean flag recreates the problem the pattern solves; a global switch on the state value reintroduces the enum design.

questions.prompt: A card terminal reports 'approved' for sale 17 and, because of a slow network, sends the same callback again 30 ms later while a third copy arrives concurrently. The machine must dispense once and capture once. Which design achieves that?
choices: Check whether the machine is currently in AwaitingCard and reject copies that find any other state with an error
Ignore duplicates by sleeping 100 ms and re-reading the state
Hold one global lock across dispense and capture and run the handler for every copy
Key on the sale ID: the first caller claims the effects under the lock, later copies return success without acting
questions.explanation: Look up the sale by its ID and decide from the sale's status, claiming the right to dispense under the lock so exactly one caller performs the effects; duplicates return success without acting. Keying only on the machine's current state fails because duplicates see different states depending on timing. Returning an error to duplicates makes the terminal retry again and page someone. A global lock held across the dispense and capture serialises the calls but blocks every other caller and still needs sale-level dedupe, because a duplicate arriving after completion would re-run the effects.

questions.prompt: A card sale expired after 60 s with nothing dispensed. At 75 s the terminal's 'approved, auth A-9' callback arrives, then arrives again. What should the machine do?
choices: Ignore the callbacks; the sale already expired
Void the authorisation once and return a 'sale closed' error to every copy
Capture the payment but do not dispense, and refund later
Dispense now, since the customer paid
questions.explanation: The authorisation holds the customer's funds for an item that will never be delivered, so the machine must void it, exactly once, and answer ErrSaleClosed so the terminal stops retrying (a flag set under the lock before the gateway call makes later copies skip the void). Capturing charges for nothing; ignoring the callback leaves the hold in place until the issuer expires it and the terminal keeps retrying; dispensing late hands out an item after the customer has walked away.

questions.prompt: A bounded coin-change DP costs O(D x A x K): D denominations, A the amount in smallest units, K the maximum coins of any one denomination. For D = 4 denominations, an amount of 200 units and at most 50 coins of each kind, about how many inner-loop steps is that in the worst case?
questions.explanation: D x A x K = 4 x 200 x 50 = 40,000 steps, tens of microseconds. Dividing the amount by the gcd of the denominations (5 cents in the example machine) cuts A to 40 and the cost to 8,000 steps. Either way the cost is negligible next to a 2-second motor run.

questions.prompt: In a vending machine that rejects wrong-state events with ErrInvalidState, which statement about Snapshot() and Tick(now) is the best design?
choices: Both should return ErrInvalidState except in Idle
Both are real events and should be rejected during Dispensing like Cancel
Snapshot is a query allowed in every state; Tick is an event that is valid (and usually a no-op) in every state
Snapshot should block until the machine is Idle; Tick should panic outside HasMoney
questions.explanation: Snapshot is a query: it never changes the machine, so it is allowed in every state (a dashboard polling during a 2-second dispense must not get an error). Tick is an event but a clock ticks whether or not anything is pending, so treating it as invalid in most states would turn a routine heartbeat into noise; it is valid everywhere and acts only where a timeout applies. Rejecting both in non-Idle states would make monitoring flap; making both silently ignore wrong states loses the 'every event has one defined answer' rule only for real events, which should still return errors.

questions.prompt: For which machine is a table-driven transition map (map[state][event] -> next state) the better choice than state objects?
choices: A machine that must call slow hardware in one state and parse payments in another
Any machine used from multiple goroutines
A 3-state, 3-event workflow whose transitions are loaded from a config file
A machine with 5 states, each with different business logic and a roadmap of new payment methods
questions.explanation: A table wins when the machine is small and the transitions are the interesting part: few states and events, behaviour that is mostly 'go to the next state', or transitions loaded from configuration or generated. State objects win when each state has real, different logic (change-making here, a motor wait there, admin operations elsewhere). The other machines have rich per-state behaviour or growth ahead, where one big table of handlers loses locality and guards get awkward.

questions.prompt: A stress test samples Snapshot() on a vending machine while 12 goroutines insert coins, select and cancel. Which invariant does NOT hold at every instant in a correct implementation?
choices: Balance always equals the total value of the Escrow coins
Whenever the state is Idle, Balance is zero
Whenever the state is Dispensing, Balance is zero
No change-box coin count and no slot quantity is ever negative
questions.explanation: While a purchase is in Dispensing the customer's coins are still in escrow (they join the change box only at commit, so a failed motor can give everything back), so 'balance is zero in Dispensing' is false. Balance always equals the value of the escrow coins; Idle implies no session and balance zero; no coin count or stock quantity is ever negative. These are exactly the invariants a sampling goroutine can assert safely.

questions.prompt: A rate board stores prices as float64. A client computes an offer as 0.1 + 0.2 and another sends a bid of 0.3. The book prints both as 0.30, but the bid and the offer never trade. What is the right fix and why?
choices: Represent price as an integer number of ticks and format only at the edges
Compare prices with a small epsilon inside the matching loop
Switch the fields to float32 to avoid the extra digits
Store prices as strings and compare them lexicographically
questions.explanation: In float64, 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so 'equal' prices are not equal and the book can look crossed or locked without trading. Prices belong in integers (ticks) so equality and ordering are exact; rounding at the display edge only. Comparing with an epsilon makes ordering inconsistent (not transitive), so levels would overlap. float32 is worse. Sorting by string keeps the two prices apart as well, and parsing text each time is slow and still ambiguous ('0.3' versus '0.30').

questions.prompt: A resting sell order is quoted at 100. A buy limit order at 105 arrives for the same quantity. At what price does the trade execute?
choices: 100, the resting order's price
105, the incoming order's limit
102.5, the midpoint
Either: the engine may choose
questions.explanation: Trades execute at the resting (maker) order's price: the taker's limit only bounds the worst price it accepts, so price improvement goes to the taker. 105 would charge the buyer more than the best offer; the midpoint (102.5) matches neither order's quote; and 'the later order's price' is the taker's limit, the wrong side of the same mistake.

questions.prompt: Orders A, B and C rest at price 100 in that arrival order, each for 5 lots. A trader amends A down to 2 lots at the same price. A buy of 4 lots then arrives at 100. Which fills result under price-time priority with the usual amend rules?
choices: A fills 2 lots, then B fills 2 lots
B fills 4 lots
B fills 4 lots, A is untouched because its amend counted as a new order
C fills 4 lots, because the amended order and B are both ahead of nobody
questions.explanation: Reducing quantity at the same price keeps the order's place, because nobody behind it is worse off, so A (2 lots) fills first and B fills 2 lots. Sending A to the back would punish a participant for reducing risk; the other choices would apply the rules for an increase or a price change, which do lose priority.

questions.prompt: Select ALL amends of a resting limit order that must send it to the back of the queue at its price level (or to a different level).
choices: Increase the quantity, same price
Change the price by one tick
Reduce the quantity, same price
Amend to the same quantity and price
questions.explanation: Increasing the quantity at the same price must lose priority, or a trader could queue with a tiny order and amend to a huge one. Changing the price moves the order to a different level with a fresh sequence number (and may make it trade). Reducing the quantity is safe for everyone behind it, so the order keeps its place; an amend that changes nothing obviously keeps it.

questions.prompt: A fill-or-kill buy for 50 lots arrives. The engine's match loop already mutates the book as it trades. Which design gives all-or-nothing behaviour with the least risk?
choices: Dry-run the opposite side to check the full quantity is available, then match
Match, and undo the trades if quantity is left over
Match what is available and rest the remainder, cancelling it a moment later
Treat it as an IOC order and report the shortfall
questions.explanation: Walk the opposite side first, without mutating, summing quantity at prices the order could trade at (honouring self-trade prevention); only if the total is at least 50 run the normal match loop, which is then guaranteed to fill completely. Matching first and undoing needs an undo log and has already consumed trade ids and possibly notified subscribers. Resting the remainder and cancelling it later exposes it to other orders and violates 'nothing happens'. Treating FOK as IOC leaves a partial fill, which is exactly what FOK forbids.

questions.prompt: A trade-stream subscriber reads far slower than trades are produced, and its channel buffer is full. Publishing happens inside the book's critical section. Which policy keeps matching running for everyone else and keeps the subscriber informed?
choices: Use a non-blocking send: drop the trade for that subscriber and count the drop
Block the send until the subscriber catches up
Give the subscriber an unbounded queue
Skip the slow subscriber silently without counting
questions.explanation: Drop (newest or oldest) with a counter: the engine's send never waits, memory stays bounded, and consecutive trade ids let the consumer see the gap and resync. A blocking send inside the lock freezes the book and every other subscriber behind the slow one. An unbounded queue just moves the failure to an out-of-memory crash later. Silently skipping the subscriber with no counter hides the data loss from everyone.

questions.prompt: Select ALL of these that can make two runs of the same input produce different trades from a matching engine.
choices: Choosing the next order by ranging over a map
Using time.Now() as the tie-breaker for time priority
Callers on several goroutines submitting with no sequencing or per-book lock
Breaking ties with a strictly increasing sequence counter
questions.explanation: Ranging over a Go map has a randomised order, wall-clock timestamps tie or step backwards so priority differs between runs, and two goroutines racing to submit mean the 'input order' itself is not fixed unless a lock or sequencer fixes and logs it. Breaking ties by a strictly increasing sequence number is deterministic, and integer arithmetic is exact and order-independent.

questions.prompt: A client submits an order, the network times out, and the client retries with the same order id. The first attempt had already filled completely and left the book. The engine rejects duplicate ids only while the order is resting. What happens, and what is the fix?
choices: It executes twice; dedupe on (owner, client order id) for a window and replay the original result
The retry is rejected with ErrDuplicateID, so nothing more is needed
It executes twice, which is acceptable because the client asked for it
The retry cancels the earlier fill and replaces it
questions.explanation: The id is free again once the order has left the book, so the retry is accepted as a brand-new order and executes a second time. The fix is idempotency at the boundary: dedupe on (owner, client order id) for a window and return the original outcome on replay, as with an idempotency key on a money transfer. Rejecting all reused ids ever needs unbounded memory; a faster timeout does not remove retries; and ErrDuplicateID alone cannot see an order that is gone.

questions.prompt: A book keeps resting orders in one slice and scans all of it for the best match on every fill, at about 5 ns per order scanned. It holds 50,000 resting orders. A market order sweeps 100 resting orders (100 fills). How long does the sweep take, in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: One scan costs 50,000 x 5 ns = 250,000 ns = 0.25 ms. 100 fills means 100 scans: 100 x 0.25 ms = 25 ms, all while holding the lock. With sorted price levels and FIFO lists each fill is O(1), so the same sweep is on the order of tens of microseconds.

questions.prompt: Why is a binary heap of orders with lazy deletion a poor primary structure for a book that must support cancel-by-id and a Depth query?
choices: Dead entries accumulate, and Depth and aggregate quantities need a sort of a copy
A heap cannot return the best order in less than O(n)
A heap cannot enforce time priority even with a sequence number in the key
A heap is not safe to use from one goroutine without a mutex
questions.explanation: A heap gives the best order cheaply, and lazy deletion makes cancel O(1) by marking, but dead entries stay until they surface (memory follows the cancel rate) and a heap is not sorted, so Depth(n) and per-price aggregates need a copy and a sort. A heap can find the best order in O(1) and insert in O(log n), so it is not slow for matching; it does not break time priority if keys include the sequence number; and it needs no locks any more or less than other structures.

questions.prompt: A rewards store sells a limited item with: if stock[sku] >= qty { stock[sku] -= qty; charge(member) }, called from one goroutine per request behind a mutex that protects only the map access (read, then separately write). 6,000 members tap in the first minute; the store confirms 212 orders for 200 units and the race detector reports nothing. What is the root cause?
choices: The check and the decrement are separate critical sections, so many goroutines pass the check before any of them decrements (a check-then-act race, not a data race)
The race detector is broken for map accesses
charge() is too slow, so stock must be decremented after it returns
The mutex should be an RWMutex so that readers do not block each other
questions.explanation: Every individual memory access is locked, so there is no data race for -race to find; the bug is logical: the invariant 'available >= 0' is checked in one critical section and acted on in another. The fix is to make check and effect one atomic step. Decrementing after charge() widens the window and strands stock on failures; an RWMutex lets more goroutines pass the check at once, and nothing is wrong with the race detector.

questions.prompt: To fix overselling, a developer wraps the whole redeem flow (check stock, call the points ledger, decrement) in one mutex. The ledger call takes about 800 ms. What is the best-case throughput of the store, in redemptions per second, regardless of how much stock there is?
questions.explanation: The lock admits one flow at a time and each flow holds it for about 0.8 s, so throughput is 1 / 0.8 s = 1.25 per second. With 10,000 members waiting, the last one learns the item is sold out after about 10,000 x 0.8 s, roughly 2.2 hours. The slow call must happen between reserve and commit, outside any lock.

questions.prompt: An inventory service expires reservations with a janitor goroutine that sweeps once per second. A reservation's deadline passes at 10:00:00.000. At 10:00:00.400 the payment callback calls Commit on it (Commit does not look at the clock). What happens, and what is the better design?
choices: The commit succeeds on a reservation past its deadline; apply expiry lazily from the clock at the top of every call, so Commit sees it as expired
The commit fails with ErrNotFound because the janitor already deleted it; keep the janitor and shorten its period
The commit blocks until the janitor runs; add a condition variable between them
The commit succeeds, which is correct because the janitor is the only authority on expiry
questions.explanation: Until the next sweep the stale reservation still counts and can still be committed, so stock that other customers were told was free is taken after the deadline. A lazy design makes expiry a function of the clock applied before every operation: exact at the deadline, deterministic to test with a fake clock, and no goroutine to leak. Shortening the janitor period only narrows the window; blocking Commit on the janitor adds coupling for no benefit.

questions.prompt: ReserveKeyed(key, lines, ttl) is idempotent. Select ALL behaviours that are correct.
choices: A retry with the same key and the same request returns the original reservation unchanged, including its original expiry
The same key with a different quantity returns an error instead of guessing which request was meant
A first attempt that failed with insufficient stock is remembered, so later retries with that key fail the same way
The key lookup and the reservation creation happen in one critical section, so concurrent duplicates create one reservation
questions.explanation: Replaying the recorded response is the whole point (an extended expiry on each retry would let a retrying vendor hold stock forever), a reused key with different parameters is a client bug to surface, and the lookup and creation must be atomic or two concurrent duplicates both see 'unseen key'. Failures must NOT be remembered: a transient 'out of stock' would become permanent for that key even after a restock.

questions.prompt: You give every SKU its own mutex. ReserveAll locks each SKU in the order given in the cart, keeps the locks, then checks and applies all lines. Under load, requests for {A,B} and {B,A} sometimes freeze forever. What is the smallest correct change that keeps per-SKU parallelism?
choices: Sort the cart's lines by SKU and acquire the locks in that global order, then check everything, apply everything and unlock
Use TryLock on the second SKU and release the first if it fails, retrying immediately
Add a 1-second timeout to each Lock call
Lock only the first SKU in the cart and read the others without a lock
questions.explanation: The freeze is a lock-order inversion: one cart holds A and waits for B while the other holds B and waits for A. A single global acquisition order makes a cycle impossible. TryLock-and-retry replaces deadlock with livelock and unfairness; sync.Mutex has no timeout; and reading other SKUs without their locks reintroduces check-then-act races on stock. A single mutex over the whole inventory also works and is simpler when no profile shows contention.

questions.prompt: A library's waitlist for a title is [W1 wants 3 copies, W2 wants 1]. One copy is free. A newcomer calls Reserve(title, 1). Under a strict FIFO policy, what should happen and why?
choices: The newcomer is refused: the free copy is owed to the queue, otherwise anyone calling at the right instant could starve W1
The newcomer gets the copy, because it is available and nobody holds it
W2 gets the copy, since it is the first waiter whose request fits
The newcomer is added to the end of the queue automatically and Reserve blocks until served
questions.explanation: Strict FIFO means the head keeps its place until its request can be met, and while a queue exists direct reservations of that SKU are refused so the queue cannot be bypassed. The cost is that the free unit idles behind a large head. Serving W2 is first-fit, a different policy with better utilisation that can starve large requests. Blocking Reserve on the queue would turn a non-blocking API into one with unbounded waits.

questions.prompt: Reservations are kept in a min-heap ordered by expiry; each lazy sweep pops entries whose expiry is <= now. An Extend feature updates a reservation's ExpiresAt in place and does nothing else. Reservations expire at 10 s, 20 s, 30 s and the 10 s one is extended to 60 s. At t = 25 s, what does Available show?
choices: Too low: the extended reservation sits at the heap root with a 60 s expiry, so the sweep stops there and never pops the 20 s one that should have expired
Correct: the sweep scans the whole heap each time
Too high: the extended reservation is dropped from the heap
A panic, because heap order is validated on every pop
questions.explanation: Changing a key in place breaks the heap invariant. The sweep looks only at the root, sees an expiry in the future and stops, so the 20 s hold keeps counting after its deadline. The fix is to store each element's heap index and call heap.Fix (or remove and re-push) after changing the key. Nothing validates heap order, the entry is not dropped, and a full scan would defeat the purpose of the heap.

questions.prompt: A customer's card authorisation succeeded, but when the checkout calls Commit on the stock reservation it gets ErrExpired: the hold lapsed during a slow payment page. What is the right behaviour?
choices: The inventory refuses to commit; the caller compensates by trying a fresh reservation and, if there is no stock, voiding or refunding the authorisation and telling the customer
The inventory commits anyway because the customer has already paid
The inventory silently extends the expired reservation and commits it
The caller retries Commit in a loop until it succeeds
questions.explanation: The component must never commit stock it may already have handed to someone else; that is the guarantee it exists to give. The caller owns compensation: re-reserve if units remain, otherwise void or refund and apologise. To make the race rarer, extend the hold when payment starts and size the TTL above the payment flow's p99. Committing anyway or resurrecting the hold oversells; retrying Commit on ErrExpired can never succeed.

questions.prompt: In the inventory model, Available is computed as Total - Committed - Reserved rather than stored. Select ALL reasons that justify this design.
choices: A stored copy is a second source of truth that some code path (expiry, failed cart, double release) will forget to update
The invariant Total = Committed + Reserved + Available then holds by construction
It avoids taking the lock when reading Available
The three stored counters change only together with the state transition that justifies them, which keeps the model auditable
questions.explanation: Deriving the number removes a class of drift bugs and makes the invariant trivially true; limiting writes to the three counters, each tied to a transition, makes the model easy to reason about and test. It does not avoid locking: computing Available still reads shared counters and must apply lazy expiry first, so it takes the same lock as everything else.

questions.prompt: A vendor adapter sends POST /v1/verifications (no idempotency key). The connection resets after the full body was written. About 12% of the time the vendor had already processed the request before the reset. What should a retry wrapper do?
choices: Return the error without retrying: the outcome is unknown, and repeating an unkeyed POST can create a duplicate
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, because connection resets are transient
Retry once, immediately, because the first attempt probably never reached the vendor
Retry only if the response status was 5xx; resets are safe to ignore
questions.explanation: After the body is written, a reset means the vendor may or may not have acted, and the client cannot tell which. Repeating a non-idempotent POST in the 'processed but unanswered' case creates a second case, charge or email. Backoff and jitter make retries gentler but not safer. 'Probably never reached the vendor' is exactly the 12% bet that produces duplicates. There is no status to inspect: a reset produces no response at all.

questions.prompt: Select ALL conditions that must hold before a retry wrapper may resend a request after a 503 response.
choices: The method is idempotent (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS) or the request carries an idempotency key
The request body can be replayed (no body, or GetBody is set)
The caller's context has not ended and attempts remain
The response body was larger than 4 KiB
questions.explanation: Safety (idempotent method or key), replayability (a consumed body cannot be sent again), and the caller still wanting an answer with attempts left are all required. The response size is irrelevant to whether a resend is safe: the wrapper drains at most 4 KiB of a discarded response so the connection can be reused, but that is a resource matter, not a retry condition.

questions.prompt: A member app, a gateway and a vendor adapter each retry a failed call up to 3 attempts in total. The vendor fails every request during an outage, and the platform sends 200 first requests per second. What is the worst-case load on the vendor, in requests per second?
questions.explanation: Attempts multiply across layers: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 attempts per original request, so 200 x 27 = 5,400 req/s. Retrying in only one layer would give 200 x 3 = 600 req/s; a 10% retry budget in that layer would hold it near 220 req/s.

questions.prompt: 10,000 clients lose their connection to a service at the same instant and all retry with delay = 1s, 2s, 4s (no randomness). What does the service see?
choices: The entire population arriving together at t = 1s, 3s, 7s: synchronised spikes that never spread out
A smooth arrival rate, because the delays double each time
Arrivals spread uniformly over each interval, as with full jitter
Only the clients whose timers happen to fire first, as the OS schedules them
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff spaces the waves further apart but keeps every client on the same schedule, so each wave is the whole surviving population at once: a thundering herd that can knock the service over again as it recovers. Randomising the delay (full jitter: uniform in [0, ceiling)) de-synchronises clients and turns the spikes into a rate of about clients divided by the ceiling. Doubling alone does not smooth anything, and timers fire at the same wall-clock moment, not in some scheduler order.

questions.prompt: Your resilient client is built as Chain(transport, retrier, breaker, bulkhead). The vendor goes down. A colleague proposes moving the breaker outside the retrier: Chain(transport, breaker, retrier, bulkhead). Compared with your order, what changes?
choices: The breaker sees one outcome per logical request instead of per attempt, so it trips later, and each half-open probe runs a full retry loop
Nothing observable: the breaker still counts every attempt
The breaker trips earlier, because it sees only the final failure of each request
Retries stop entirely, because the breaker consumes the errors
questions.explanation: Outside the retrier, the breaker only sees the final result of each request after all attempts. With 3 attempts per request it needs roughly three times as many real failures to trip, and a recovering vendor gets a whole retry loop (up to 3 requests) per probe instead of one. It does not trip earlier, retries still happen inside it, and the attempts are no longer individually counted.

questions.prompt: A breaker admits request A while closed. A is slow. Other requests fail, the breaker opens, the cooldown passes, and one probe is admitted in half-open. Now A completes successfully. What should the breaker do with A's result?
choices: Ignore it: A was admitted in an earlier state, so its result must not decide the probe's verdict
Close the circuit: a success proves the vendor is healthy
Count it as a second probe success and close once K is reached
Reopen the circuit, because a request completed during half-open
questions.explanation: A's success reflects the vendor as it was when A started, before the failures that opened the circuit. Using it as evidence about the half-open phase could close the circuit while the real probe is still pending. Tagging each admitted request with a generation number that changes on every state transition lets the breaker drop stale results with a single comparison. Closing, counting it as a probe, or reopening all let results from the wrong era change the state.

questions.prompt: Select ALL outcomes that should count as a FAILURE for a vendor circuit breaker.
choices: A connection reset or a per-attempt timeout
A 503 Service Unavailable response
A 404 Not Found response
The member closing the app, cancelling the request context
questions.explanation: Transport errors (including timeouts) and 5xx responses signal vendor trouble. A 404, like other 4xx responses, says the request was wrong, not that the vendor is unhealthy; counting it would let a burst of bad lookups open the circuit. A cancellation by the caller says nothing about the vendor at all and is ignored.

questions.prompt: A bulkhead limits a vendor to 10 concurrent calls. Its Wrap releases the slot as soon as RoundTrip returns the response. Under load, the vendor connection count is far above 10. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Callers are still reading response bodies on connections the bulkhead no longer counts; the slot should be held until the body is closed
The semaphore channel was created with the wrong capacity
Go's http.Transport ignores request limits
The bulkhead should be placed outside the retrier so it sees fewer requests
questions.explanation: An HTTP connection stays busy until the response body has been read or closed, so releasing the slot when headers arrive lets many bodies be in flight at once. Wrapping the body so Close releases the slot (exactly once) keeps the count honest. A wrong semaphore capacity would show up as a constant mismatch in simple tests, not only under slow bodies. Transport limits are separate and do not cause this. Placing the bulkhead outside the retrier makes it hold slots through backoff sleeps, which is a different problem.

questions.prompt: Your RoundTripper creates a per-attempt context with context.WithTimeout and writes defer cancel() right after calling next.RoundTrip. In production, callers intermittently get 'context canceled' while reading a response body that looked fine. Why?
choices: The deferred cancel fires when RoundTrip returns, which cancels the request context while the caller is still reading the body; cancel on body Close instead
The timeout was too short; raising it removes the problem
http.Transport cancels bodies on keep-alive connections
context.WithTimeout cancels itself when the parent has no deadline
questions.explanation: The transport ties the body read to the request's context, so cancelling that context when RoundTrip returns aborts any later read. The cancel function belongs in the body's Close (and in error paths). A longer timeout does not help because the cancel is explicit, not a timeout. Keep-alive handling and parentless contexts are unrelated.

questions.prompt: A retry budget deposits 0.1 token per request and each retry costs 1 token. Your retry loop checks attempts remaining, then the deadline, then withdraws a token. Which placement of the withdrawal is correct, and why?
choices: After all the other gates, immediately before the retry happens, so a token is spent only on a retry that will be made
First, before any other check, so denied requests are rejected as cheaply as possible
Never withdraw; deposit only, since the budget is a rate limit on first attempts
In the breaker, because only the breaker knows when the vendor is struggling
questions.explanation: If the withdrawal comes before the 'attempts left' or deadline checks, requests that were never going to retry still drain the bucket, so real retries get denied later and the budget no longer matches actual retry volume. The budget gates retries only (first attempts always run), and it belongs in the retrier, which is the one component that decides to repeat a request.

questions.prompt: Your shortener's Service must work with a memory store today, a sharded store next week, and a test fake that can inject failures. A teammate proposes one Storage interface with Put, Get, Delete, FindByURL, IncrClicks, ListByOwner and Search 'so we never have to change it'. What is the best response?
choices: Define a small interface next to the Service containing only the methods it calls (Put, Get, Delete); add optional second interfaces if a capability is needed later
Accept the wide interface: one contract is simpler than several small ones
Use an abstract factory that builds a different Store per feature
Skip the interface and take the concrete memory store, then refactor when a second store appears
questions.explanation: Consumer-side interfaces list only what the consumer calls, so every fake and every new backend implements three methods, and adding aliases, TTL, stats and sharding in later stages changes nothing. The wide interface forces every implementation (and every test fake) to support methods the Service does not use and turns each 'later' method into a promise. An abstract factory adds a layer without removing any coupling. A concrete dependency makes the failure-injection and collision tests impossible to write without a rewrite.

questions.prompt: Shorten is idempotent via a map[url]code. The code locks the mutex to read the map, unlocks, mints a code and stores the record, then locks again to write the map. Fifty goroutines shorten the same new URL at once. What can happen, and what does go test -race report?
choices: Several codes and records are created for one URL, some callers get different codes; -race reports nothing because every map access is locked
A data race on the map is reported, but the results are always correct
Exactly one code is created because the mutex serializes the map accesses
The program deadlocks because the mutex is acquired twice in one call
questions.explanation: The mutex protects each map access but not the sequence 'check, mint, store, record', so several goroutines can all see a miss. That is a race condition (check-then-act), not a data race, so the race detector stays silent. The result is orphaned records and inconsistent answers. The mutex is released between the two acquisitions, so there is no self-deadlock, and per-access locking does not serialize the whole operation.

questions.prompt: An alias has expired. Claimants A and B each run: Put, see ErrExists, Get shows the record expired, Delete, Put. A completes its Delete and Put successfully; B then runs its Delete and Put. What is the outcome, and the smallest correct fix for a single process?
choices: B deletes A's fresh record and both are told they own the alias; hold a per-alias lock across read, delete and put (and in the public Delete)
A's Put fails because the store's Put is atomic, so only B wins; no fix is needed
B's Delete returns ErrNotFound and B gets ErrAliasTaken; no fix is needed
Both Puts fail, so the alias is lost; retry the whole sequence in a loop
questions.explanation: The store's Put is atomic, but Delete is unconditional: B applies a decision based on an old read ('the record is expired') to A's new record. Both calls report success and the alias points at B's URL. Serializing the whole read-delete-put per alias (the same lock that guards the public Delete) removes the interleaving; across processes you would need a conditional delete. The other outcomes ignore that B's Delete finds A's record present and removes it.

questions.prompt: A shortener on a bank's domain must only redirect to ordinary web pages. Select ALL inputs it should reject.
choices: javascript:alert(document.cookie)
https://mybank.example@evil.example/login
data:text/html;base64,PHNjcmlwdD4=
HTTPS://Example.COM:443/Path?q=1#top
questions.explanation: javascript: and data: URLs are not web pages and run script in the victim's browser. A URL with user info looks like it belongs to mybank.example but the browser connects to evil.example, a classic phishing trick. The last input is a normal https URL: a case-insensitive scheme and host, the default port and a query are legitimate and should be normalized to https://example.com/Path?q=1#top, not rejected.

questions.prompt: URL u1 was shortened to code 'id-1' and recorded in the dedupe index. Then 'id-1' was deleted, and a different URL u2 claimed 'id-1' as a custom alias. Now Shorten(u1) is called. The index still says u1 -> id-1. What should Shorten do?
choices: Read the record for id-1, notice it points at u2, drop the stale index entry and mint a new code for u1
Return id-1, because the index is the source of truth for URL to code
Return an error because u1 is already registered
Clear the whole index and start again
questions.explanation: The index is only a hint; the store owns the truth. Validating a hit (record exists, not expired, record.URL equals the URL) catches deleted, expired and re-claimed codes. Returning id-1 would send u1's users to u2's page. An error blames the caller for the service's own stale state, and flushing the whole index throws away every valid hint.

questions.prompt: Short codes are 6 random base-62 characters (62^6 is about 5.7e10 possible codes). Using the birthday approximation sqrt(pi/2 * N), about how many links are created before the first collision is expected? Answer as a count.
questions.explanation: sqrt(pi/2 * 5.7e10) = sqrt(8.9e10), about 3e5 links. The first collision arrives long before the space is anywhere near full, so a random-code service needs a collision path (retry with a bound) and a test that forces it. At 7 characters (3.5e12) it moves to about 2.4e6 links; it never goes away.

questions.prompt: Your Service tests all pass against MemoryStore. You write a ShardedStore whose Put checks for the code under a read lock, releases it, then takes the write lock to insert. All Service tests still pass. What catches the bug?
choices: A shared Store contract suite that hammers Put of one code from many goroutines and requires exactly one winner
The Service's own parallel-Shorten test, which always fails when the store is wrong
go vet
Nothing can; atomicity cannot be tested
questions.explanation: The Service serializes many calls with its own per-key locks, so a non-atomic Put is usually never exercised concurrently through it. A contract test that targets the store directly (32 goroutines Put the same code, exactly one may succeed) does exercise it, and the same suite is the proof that any new backend is a drop-in. go vet does not reason about check-then-act across lock regions, and atomicity is testable by contention.

questions.prompt: You switch the shortener to random IDs. The collision-retry code path would only run about once per 300,000 links in production. How do you test it?
choices: Inject a scripted ID generator that returns 7, 7, 7, 8 with a store already holding the code for 7, and assert on Put attempts and the final code
Run Shorten a million times in a loop and hope a collision occurs
Mock the random number generator package-wide with a global variable
Do not test it; the store's unique constraint guarantees correctness
questions.explanation: A scripted generator through the IDGenerator seam makes the collision certain and the test deterministic (3 failed attempts, then success; or ErrCollisionExhausted with MaxAttempts 3). A million-iteration loop is slow, flaky and still unlikely to hit the path at 6 characters. A global override leaks between tests and is not a seam. The store's unique constraint only detects the collision; the Service's response to it (retry, bound, no leftover state) is the code that needs the test.

questions.prompt: Resolve calls store.Get, which returns an error that is neither ErrNotFound nor a context error (a connection reset). What should Resolve return?
choices: That error (possibly wrapped), not ErrNotFound
ErrNotFound, since the caller only needs to know the link is unavailable
An empty URL and nil error so the HTTP handler redirects to a default page
ErrExists, because the record may still be present
questions.explanation: Only ErrNotFound means 'no such link'. Reporting an outage as not found lets callers return a 404 and caches may remember it for a link that exists. The caller must be able to tell 'missing' from 'try again'. Returning an empty URL with nil is a silent failure, and ErrExists means something else entirely (a create-if-absent conflict).

questions.prompt: A product manager wants per-link click analytics from the redirect service. The HTTP handler currently answers every redirect with 301. What is the problem and the fix?
choices: 301 is cacheable by browsers and intermediaries, so repeat visits may never reach the service; use 302 or 307 when you need to count or change the target
301 cannot carry a Location header, so redirects fail; use 200 with a meta refresh
301 forces the service to keep a session per visitor; use 302 to avoid cookies
There is no problem; caches always revalidate redirects with the origin
questions.explanation: A permanent redirect may be cached for a long time, so later clicks are served without contacting you: the counts undercount and you cannot retarget or delete the link for those clients. A temporary redirect (302/307) is not cached by default, at the price of more requests. 301 carries Location like any redirect, has nothing to do with sessions, and caches do not necessarily revalidate.

questions.prompt: A game leaderboard has 2 million players. Scores change constantly, and the product needs top-100, 'what is my rank?' and 'show me the 5 players above and below me'. Which structure serves all three in O(log n) per operation?
choices: A balanced tree (treap, skip list with spans) where each node knows its subtree size
A binary min-heap of size 100, updated on every score change
A sorted slice with binary search and copy-based insertion
A hash map from player to score, sorted on demand
questions.explanation: Subtree sizes turn 'how many players are ahead of this key' and 'give me positions 1,000,000..1,000,009' into one root-to-leaf walk, and updates are delete+insert in O(log n). A size-100 heap can give the top 100 but cannot rank an arbitrary player or reposition one whose score dropped out of it. A sorted slice finds positions in O(log n) but each insert moves O(n) elements (about 2 million x 32 bytes). Sorting a map on demand is O(n log n) per query.

questions.prompt: Someone proposes keeping the top-k with a min-heap of size k, plus 'lazy deletion' for score changes (push a new entry, ignore stale ones when popped). Which requirement does this design fundamentally NOT meet?
choices: Rank(player) for a player outside the heap, in better than O(n)
TopK(k) in O(k log k)
Handling scores that only increase
Handling ties deterministically
questions.explanation: A heap only orders its root: it has no notion of 'how many entries are better than this one', so ranking an arbitrary player means scanning (or sorting) everything. TopK is exactly what heaps are good at, and monotonically increasing scores plus lazy deletion are workable. Ties are just part of the comparison key, so a heap handles them like any other ordering.

questions.prompt: Players are loaded in strictly ascending score order (1, 2, 3, ...) into a leaderboard built on a plain, unbalanced binary search tree. What happens?
choices: The tree degenerates into a linked list: every insert and rank query costs O(n)
Nothing: a BST is always O(log n) on average
Inserts get faster because each new key goes to the same side
Only deletes are affected
questions.explanation: Each new key is the largest so far and becomes the right child of the previous one, producing a chain of depth n. 'O(log n) on average' holds only for random insertion order, and real data (IDs, timestamps, scores from a ramp-up) is often sorted. A treap's random priorities (or a skip list's random levels, or red-black rotations) keep the expected depth logarithmic whatever order the keys arrive in.

questions.prompt: Players Ann and Bob both have 500 points. Ann reached 500 yesterday; Bob reached it a minute ago, then lost and regained 1 point so that he is back at 500. In the reference ordering ('whoever reached the score first ranks higher'), who is ahead, and why is this a product decision rather than a technical one?
choices: Ann, because Bob's current 500 was reached later. Someone must decide whether 'reached' resets when a score leaves and returns
Bob, because he was active more recently
They share rank 1, because a leaderboard must always show equal scores as equal
Whichever was inserted first into the data structure, which is unspecified
questions.explanation: The ordering key is (score, time the player reached that score). Bob left 500 and came back, so his arrival time is newer. Other defensible policies exist: competition ranking (equal scores share a rank and the next rank is skipped), tie-break by name, or by first time ever at that score. They give different pages, different reward cutoffs and different support tickets, so it is a rule to agree with the product owner and then test, not an implementation detail. Leaving it unspecified makes paging unstable.

questions.prompt: A client pages through a live leaderboard with Page(offset, 50), fetching offset 0, then 50, then 100 while scores keep changing. A user near rank 60 gains 40 places between the first and second request. What can the client observe?
choices: The same player on two pages, or a player never shown, because the ranking shifted between requests
Nothing unusual: offset paging is stable under updates
An error, because the offset no longer exists
The pages are always sorted but may be shorter
questions.explanation: Offsets count positions in the ranking at the moment of each request, and positions move when others pass each other. A player who moves from rank 60 to rank 20 after page 1 was shown is missed on page 2 if you started past it, and a player pushed from rank 49 to 51 appears on both pages. This is the same offset-pagination drift as in the API-design module. Fixes: page through one Snapshot (point-in-time copy) for the whole session, or use a cursor on the sort key (score, reached-at) so the next page starts after the last row seen.

questions.prompt: A leaderboard is split over 8 shards by hash of the player name. To compute the global top 10 you ask each shard for its top 10 and merge. How many entries per shard are needed for this to be correct, and why?
choices: 10: a player in the global top 10 has fewer than 10 players ahead of them overall, so fewer than 10 inside their own shard
10 / 8 rounded up, because the top 10 is spread evenly over the shards
All of them: a shard cannot know which of its players are globally good
20: one extra page as a safety margin
questions.explanation: If a player has fewer than 10 players ahead of them globally, they certainly have fewer than 10 ahead of them within their own shard, so they are in their shard's top 10. All 10 global winners could even live in one shard, so taking 10/8 per shard would drop some. Fetching everything defeats the purpose, and a safety margin of 20 is waste with no correctness benefit.

questions.prompt: You shard a leaderboard by hash(player) over 16 shards, each its own board with its own lock. Select ALL statements that are true.
choices: Writers to different shards no longer contend on one lock
Rank(player) must consult every shard, not just the player's own
TopK across shards reflects one single instant, because each shard is internally consistent
Tie-breaking by 'who reached the score first' needs one logical clock shared by all shards
questions.explanation: Hashing spreads writes over 16 locks. Rank counts players ahead of this one, and they may live in any shard. Ties across shards are only comparable if arrival order is a single global sequence, otherwise two shards can each hand out 'seq 7'. TopK reads the shards one after another, so it is a merge of 16 slightly different instants; a true global snapshot needs extra coordination (a global version or briefly locking all shards).

questions.prompt: A daily leaderboard must reset at midnight. Which design is easiest to test deterministically and has no goroutine to leak?
choices: Inject a clock; compute the window index from it and rotate lazily on the first call that sees a later index
Start a goroutine with time.Ticker(24h) that swaps the board
Call time.Now() directly in each method and compare the date
Use time.AfterFunc to schedule the reset and cancel it on Close
questions.explanation: With an injected clock a test advances time by assigning a number; rotation is a pure function of (clock, state) and needs no background goroutine, so there is nothing to stop on shutdown and nothing to race with. A ticker goroutine needs Close, can fire in the middle of an Add and cannot be tested without waiting a real day. Calling time.Now() directly makes tests depend on the wall clock. AfterFunc has the same lifecycle and testability costs as the ticker.

questions.prompt: A daily leaderboard rotates lazily. Nobody calls it on Tuesday and Wednesday; on Thursday someone adds a score. A client asks for 'yesterday's board' (Previous(1)). What should the lazy design return, and what does the alternative cost?
choices: An empty board for Wednesday, by closing the skipped days as empty windows; this keeps Previous(n) meaning 'n calendar days ago' at the cost of creating up to keep empty boards
Monday's board, since it is the most recent one that had data; this is cheaper but 'yesterday' no longer means yesterday
An error, because nothing happened on Wednesday
Thursday's board, since it is the current one
questions.explanation: Previous(n) is a calendar question, so a day without activity must be an empty window, otherwise a client asking for yesterday silently receives data from three days ago. The cost is bounded: at most 'keep' empty boards are created however long the gap was. Returning Monday's board is a legitimate but different product semantics ('last active window') and should be an explicit second method. An error makes the caller handle a case that is really just an empty board.

questions.prompt: A leaderboard keeps 10 million players in a balanced tree with one node per player, about 64 bytes per node (record, priority, size, two pointers) plus about 50 bytes for the name-to-record map entry. Roughly how much memory does the structure use? Answer in megabytes (decimal).
questions.explanation: 10,000,000 players x (64 B node + 50 B map entry) = 1.14 x 10^9 B, about 1.1 GB. That fits in one machine's RAM but is big enough to matter for snapshots: an O(n) Snapshot copy needs another 1.1 GB and several hundred milliseconds, which is why large boards use a persistent tree (O(1) snapshot, O(log n) new nodes per write), Redis-style sorted sets, or sharding.

questions.prompt: A cache cluster of 4 nodes routes with hash(key) % N. You add a 5th node. Roughly what percentage of keys are now routed to a different node than before?
questions.explanation: A key keeps its node only if hash % 4 == hash % 5. Over one period of lcm(4, 5) = 20 hash values that holds for residues 0-3, so 4 of 20 = 20% stay and about 80% move. A consistent-hash ring would move only about 1/5 = 20% (all of them to the new node), which is why the modulo scheme turns a routine resize into a near-total cache flush.

questions.prompt: On a consistent-hash ring, a new node is added. Which statement about the keys that change owner is correct?
choices: Every key that changes owner moves to the new node; no key moves between the existing nodes
Keys are redistributed evenly among all nodes, old and new
Only keys that were on the new node's neighbours move, and they move to the neighbours' neighbours
No keys move, because the ring is stable by construction
questions.explanation: Existing nodes' points do not move when a node is added, so a key's owner can only change if one of the new node's points becomes its closest point clockwise; that point belongs to the new node. Even redistribution is what a modulo scheme (accidentally) does, and it moves far more keys than necessary. The new node must receive its share of keys, so 'no keys move' is wrong, and keys never hop between old nodes.

questions.prompt: A 5-node ring with one virtual node per node shows one node holding over twice the mean load and another almost nothing. Which change most directly fixes this, and why?
choices: Give each node roughly 100-200 virtual nodes: load variation shrinks about like 1/sqrt(v) because each node's load becomes a sum of many small arcs
Use a larger hash space such as 128 bits; the extra bits make the arcs equal
Sort the nodes by name before adding them; the order determines arc length
Add a second ring and use whichever node is less loaded
questions.explanation: With one point per node the arc lengths are essentially random and unequal. With v points per node each node owns a sum of v random arcs, whose relative spread falls like 1/sqrt(v) (measured about 0.70 for v=1, 0.24 for v=10, 0.064 for v=150). A bigger hash space does not make arcs more equal, insertion order does not matter on a correct ring (positions depend only on names), and two rings would destroy the single-owner property.

questions.prompt: A cache client with R=1 skips a node it has marked down and routes that node's keys to the next healthy node clockwise. Select ALL consequences that are true.
choices: The service keeps working with a lower hit ratio instead of returning errors
With many virtual nodes the dead node's load spreads over all survivors rather than one neighbour
When the node returns, values written during the outage are on the neighbour while the ring points at the returned node, so those keys miss once until their TTL expires
The data on the dead node is migrated to the neighbour automatically
questions.explanation: Failover keeps the cache usable and, with virtual nodes, each survivor absorbs only about 1/(N-1) of the dead node's keys. After recovery the ring routes reads back to the returned node, which is empty for those keys, so they miss once; the stranded copies on the neighbour are harmless and expire. Nothing copies the dead node's data anywhere, because a cache does not replicate on failure; that would need R>1 or hinted handoff.

questions.prompt: During a resize, a Get that misses on the new owner B reads the value v1 from the old owner A and copies it forward. Before the copy, another goroutine stores v2 for the same key on B. Which copy-forward is correct?
choices: Backend.Add (set-if-absent): it fails because B already has a value, so v2 survives
Backend.Set: the reader's value is the one that was read last, so it is freshest
Backend.Set followed by Delete on A, so that only one copy remains
Skip the copy entirely and always read through A for the whole grace window
questions.explanation: Anything already on B was written after the migration started, so it is at least as new as A's copy; Add refuses to overwrite it. A plain Set loses the update and serves stale v1 until the TTL. Deleting A afterwards does not repair B. Reading through A forever works only if writes also go to A, doubles reads on every moved key, and defeats the purpose of the migration.

questions.prompt: One key receives 40% of all cache traffic and its node is saturated. Which change actually helps?
choices: A short-TTL in-process cache in each client, or reading that key from several replicas or key copies
Increasing the number of virtual nodes per node to 1,000
Switching to a better hash function so the key lands on a less loaded node
Enabling bounded loads based on the number of keys per node
questions.explanation: Hashing balances keys, not requests per key: one key maps to one node however many virtual nodes exist, and a better hash only changes which node it lands on. Bounded loads counted in keys per node does not see request skew, and even request-based bounds cannot split a single key. Absorbing the reads before they reach the node (local cache) or spreading copies of the key across nodes does.

questions.prompt: Consistent hashing with bounded loads, factor c = 1.25: 10,000 distinct keys are placed on 8 nodes. What is the maximum number of keys any one node may receive, i.e. ceil(c x keys / nodes)?
questions.explanation: Average load is 10,000 / 8 = 1,250 keys; with c = 1.25 each node's capacity is ceil(1.25 x 1,250) = ceil(1,562.5) = 1,563. Any node that is full passes the key on to the next node clockwise that has room, so no node exceeds 1,563 even if the keys are heavily skewed.
