questions.prompt: During a grace window after adding a node, a client deletes key k. k currently exists only on the old owner A: it has not been read since the resize, so it was never migrated to the new owner B. A later Get(k) must still report 'not found'. What must Delete do?
choices: Delete k on the new owner and also on the previous owners that no longer own it, so the next miss cannot migrate the old copy back
Delete k only on the new owner; the old owner's copy expires on its own
Delete k only on the old owner, since it holds the authoritative copy
Nothing: migration copies only values newer than the delete
questions.explanation: If the old owner keeps its copy, the next read misses on B, finds k on A and copies it forward: the deleted value is resurrected. Deleting on both generations during the window prevents it. Waiting for expiry leaves a window of wrong answers, deleting only on A leaves a copy on B in other cases, and migration has no notion of timestamps, so it cannot know the copy is older than the delete. A delete racing a migration read can still resurrect once; tombstones or the TTL on migrated entries bound that.

questions.prompt: In a 90-minute machine-coding round you have been designing on paper for 30 minutes and nothing compiles yet. What is the best correction?
choices: Stop, commit to the simplest model that supports the likely next requirement, and get one method plus its test running within minutes
Keep designing until the class diagram covers every requirement the interviewer might add
Switch to pseudocode for the remaining methods so the structure is clear, then type it all at the end
Ask the interviewer to extend the time box so the design can be completed
questions.explanation: Design beyond about 10 minutes is guessing about requirements you have not seen, and untested code is a hypothesis: the sooner something runs, the sooner wrong assumptions surface. Covering every imaginable requirement never terminates, writing pseudocode defers the same risk to the end, and asking for more time signals poor time management without fixing the cause.

questions.prompt: At minute 50 the interviewer says: 'make it safe for concurrent use.' You have 25 minutes left and a sequential implementation. What is the best first move?
choices: State a one-mutex-per-instance model, list the shared state, lock the exported methods, and fix check-then-act and callbacks
Convert the design to channels and goroutines because Go prefers sharing memory by communicating
Wrap every method, public and private, in the mutex, so nothing can be missed
Replace the maps with sync.Map and the counters with atomics, then run the tests
questions.explanation: A short, stated lock model is the cheapest correct change: exported methods lock for their whole body, helpers assume the lock is held, and any check-then-act or user callback is restructured. A redesign around channels risks ending with neither version working. Locking every method including private ones makes public-calls-public self-deadlocks likely. sync.Map and atomics protect single operations, not multi-step invariants, so check-then-act bugs survive them.

questions.prompt: You can write only a few tests before the interviewer runs your code. Select ALL that belong in the first few.
choices: A table-driven test of invalid inputs and invalid state transitions using errors.Is
An end-state invariant check after N goroutines hammer the exported API, run under -race
An expiry or timing test that uses an injected clock
A test that sleeps two seconds to let a background goroutine finish
questions.explanation: The error table, the concurrent invariant test and the injected-clock time test give the most signal per minute and are deterministic. Sleeping for real time is slow and flaky, and the interviewer watches you wait; replace it with events, channels or a fake clock and a timeout on every wait.

questions.prompt: At minute 80 you realise your Rename is two separate critical sections, so a concurrent observer can see the file in neither place. The interviewer has not noticed. What do you do?
choices: Say so, scope the fix (one critical section), apply it if time allows and add a regression test with a concurrent observer
Say nothing: the tests pass and the interviewer might not run -race
Rewrite the storage layer with immutable snapshots so the problem cannot recur
Add a comment in the code and move on to cleanup
questions.explanation: Interviewers score judgment under pressure: finding, scoping and fixing your own flaw shows the review habit the job needs. Silence risks being caught by the closing discussion or -race. A late rewrite breaks green tests for an uncertain gain, and a comment documents the bug without fixing or testing it.

questions.prompt: A rate-limiter-like component reads time.Now() directly and its tests call time.Sleep to cross a window boundary. Which change gives the most for a timed round?
choices: Inject the clock as a func() time.Time at construction and advance a fake clock in tests
Define a Clock interface with Now, After, Tick, Sleep and NewTimer methods up front
Use a package-level variable for time.Now and swap it in tests
Keep the sleeps but shorten them to a few milliseconds
questions.explanation: A function value injected at construction is the smallest seam: deterministic tests, no global state, and parallel tests cannot interfere. A large Clock interface is premature and must be faked in full. A swapped package variable is global mutable state that races under parallel tests. Shorter sleeps still depend on scheduling and make tests flaky under -race.

questions.prompt: You must choose a concurrency model for an order book that must be deterministic and replayable, with one writer per symbol and many symbols. Which model fits best?
choices: A single-writer goroutine (or one mutex) per symbol, so each book processes its events in one total order
One global mutex around all symbols, because it is simplest
Lock-free CAS loops on each price level, to maximise throughput
A sync.Map of orders updated concurrently by any goroutine
questions.explanation: Determinism requires a total order of events per book, which a single writer or per-book lock provides, while different symbols stay independent and run in parallel. One global lock needlessly serialises independent symbols. Lock-free level updates make price-time priority and invariants hard to guarantee. A shared map updated by any goroutine gives no ordering at all.

questions.prompt: You are 10 minutes behind at the halfway mark of a 90-minute round. Which cut is correct?
choices: Drop an optional method or secondary error case; keep invariant tests, the concurrency pass and the spoken note
Skip the tests for the remaining methods and write them at the end
Skip the concurrency pass because the interviewer may not ask
Stop and restart with a simpler design
questions.explanation: Cut breadth, not quality gates: tests of invariants, the concurrency pass and the narration are what the rubric scores. Deferring tests moves debugging to the end where it is most expensive, skipping the pass risks a visible failure under -race, and restarting discards the work that already runs.

questions.prompt: A realistic sustained pace is about 6 lines per minute of tested code. In a 90-minute round, roughly 35 minutes go to actually writing code. About how many lines (code plus tests) will you produce? Answer in lines.
questions.explanation: 6 lines/min x 35 min = 210 lines of tested code. The rest of the 90 minutes goes to questions, design, debugging and talking. That is why a solution of 250-400 lines plus tests is the upper end of what a round can contain, and why scoping and cutting matter.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the headings of the five-part concurrency note you should be able to give for any code you wrote.
choices: Shared state and owners
Bounds (queues, goroutines, memory)
Lifecycle (what starts, what stops, what Close waits for)
Failure handling (panics, slow consumers, dependency errors)
Evidence (which test proves which property)
Programming language rationale
questions.explanation: The note covers shared state and owners, bounds, lifecycle, failure handling and evidence. Why the language was chosen is not part of it: it says nothing about whether the code is safe or how you know.
